utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you were questioning Mr. Semenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. MR. MEVLUDIN SEMENOVIC, recalled Examined by MR. TIEGER, continued.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Semenovic, you understand that you are still under oath, do you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you may begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. (To the witness): Good morning, Mr. Semenovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Before yesterday's adjournment, you were testifying about the measures imposed against the Muslim and Croat communities in Prijedor after the military takeover. Did members of the SDA attempt to meet with the coup leaders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we tried that on several occasions and at various levels. The Chairman of the party tried to do that and some members of the Executive Board as well, and also some party institutions in local communes. The last successful attempt was an agreement to have a meeting between the leaders of the SDS and the SDA parties. That meeting was held around either 15th or 16th April.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Semenovic ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is May, I am sorry, May. The meeting was held in the SDS offices. It was difficult to go to the meeting because the territories where non-Serb population lived were completely blocked, but conduct was ensured through Serbian checkpoints by telephone. SDS guaranteed for people to be able to go to the meeting. I was at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Semenovic, when you say "the last successful attempt", did you mean by successful the fact that you were able to arrange a meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the success was to ask the SDS to talk and they accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did the SDA officials meet together in advance of the meeting to discuss things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Part of the leadership managed to meet, but it was impossible for the whole leadership to meet, because movement was impaired and in some parts impossible. So only part of the leadership was at that meeting, but of course after the oral acknowledgment of the Chairman of the Party and other members of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you able to get into the SDA party headquarters before that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we were not able to do it. When we arrived to Prijedor, I started from Kozarac where I lived, that is, from Trnopolje to Kozarac, and then some of us from the leadership of the Party, we managed to come to the offices of the Party. We tried to go inside, but the lock was changed. It was in the early hours of the afternoon, around 1400 hours. The key we had could not open the door any more. After several attempts in knocking at the door, a lady who used to be a cleaner there, she was a cleaner of one of the municipal departments on the first floor, she said it was not possible for us to go in there. There was nothing else we could look for there and she was going to call the police. After several attempts, we abandoned the idea and then we went towards the SDS offices which at that time were on the ground floor of the neighbouring building. On our way from the SDA offices to the SDS offices, the police came. There were four policemen. Two policemen asked our identity cards.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: After showing the policemen your identity cards, were you able to get into SDS headquarters and meet with SDS officials?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they checked our papers, some leaders of the SDA were against these checking of identity, because they up to recently then were civil servants in the Municipal Assembly, but the police protested. After some metres where we were walking altogether with the policemen, we arrived in front of the SDS offices building. The Chairman was there and we said there was no point for the police to check us, and he answered, "We could forget about it and he said, "Forget about it all".

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Which SDA officials were at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we arrived at the offices, Mr. Simo Miskovic was there, Mr. Slobodan Kuruzovic, and then Dragan Kurnoga, a young woman that used to work there as an employee, and as the SDA delegation there was Professor Ilijaz Music, Mr. Meho Terzic, Mr. Becir Medunjanin, Mr. Islam Bahonjic, Mr. Mustafa Tadzic and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did the meeting begin immediately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, we wanted to start talking straightaway because we felt very unpleasantly, specially because the police asked us about our identity cards and we were not sure that we would be able to go back from the meeting. But they insisted upon us waiting for some time. Then Mr. Miskovic telephoned to the barracks. He said he talked with Messrs. Arsic and Zeljaja, the Commanders, and he said those from SDA had arrived and that, that, they could come. He invited them to come there. We were waiting and the meeting did not begin before the officers came. When the officers appeared at the door and when they sat down, Miskovic said, "Well, now we can start the meeting."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel Arsic and Commander Zeljaja were members of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When the meeting began what did SDA leaders tell the SDS delegation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For us, it was very difficult to start the meeting in such an atmosphere, because all the time they were joking from the beginning, they were laughing quite a lot. They said at first we should have a drink. Mr. Arsic took the stock. Then he offered it to everybody and then they started joking because some of the SDA leaders did not drink alcohol. Then they ordered coffee. They said, "They drink Turkish coffee". They said to the girl to make it and then to offer it to us, and after some time Professor Music was the first one to start talking. He was speaking about a difficult situation, about the fear that the people felt, how people were thrown away -- thrown out of their jobs, that something should be done, that SDA and the Bosniak Muslim people or any other people of the non-Serb nationality did not provoke such behaviour of the SDS authorities, and that we should agree on how to solve that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did any other SDA leader speak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Medunjanin spoke as a representative from Kozarac. I also spoke, but while we were speaking we were very often interrupted. All the time we were told, we were told that we were trying to start a war. For us, it was very difficult, almost impossible, situation because at those moments you really do not know how to discuss. Some of them elaborated their thesis for about 10 to 15 minutes, and then they would offer and that offer was explained lastly by Slobodan Kuruzovic. Then for the last time they repeated something offered many times, that the SDS and SDA leaders should take a bus and go to the frontline to the Republic of Croatia, because they wanted to convince us what war meant, what kind of suffering and destruction a war brings with it, so that afterwards we would change our politics. To us, it was unclear and illogical because we were in absolutely different positions. They had all the military force and armed people. We did not have anything, except for our political opinions and fighting for our own security and for our country.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What did Mr. Medunjanin tell the SDS leaders when he spoke?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At one moment during these long discussions Mr. Zeljaja was saying that the Muslims should give back their arms, that no discussions could be held without that, that they had to disarm the alleged green berets because almost all the Muslims were armed. These were his words. At one moment Mr. Medunjanin said, "Well, do you really think we have got arms?" The Commander Zeljaja answered him, "Here I have got my intelligence officer with me", and he pointed to a person none of us knew. I do not think he was from Prijedor. He said, "We have got all the information, not only that you are armed, but you have got very many weapons, not 1,000 or 2,000 rifles, Kozarac has got about 7,000 barrels. When you return 7,000 barrels, gentlemen, then we will be able to talk."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did Commander Zeljaja indicate what he would do if 7,000 weapons were not turned over to the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did. After these words of his, Mr. Medunjanin asked to speak and then Mr. Tadzic. They said it was impossible to surrender 7,000 rifles when there was not even 1,000 of them. He said, "We have got information and you, gentlemen, do not try and play with us. The Banja Luka corps is the strongest one in Europe. We have got tanks, cannons, aviation aircraft, we have got missiles, land land. We have got 30,000 soldiers. When you surrender those weapons, then we can talk. Apart from that, in Kozarac there should be a Serb flag and Serb police".

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did anybody indicate that there was pressure being mounted by people within the Serbian community to have a Serbian flag and Serbian police in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At one moment Simo Miskovic, I had a feeling that he was trying to explain why they had such a strong statement. At one moment he said, "We will not be able to hold our extremists for a long time. They cannot see that Bosnia-Herzegovina flag in Kozarac. They will make something evil."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did the SDA propose any measures to reduce tension or moderate the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We looked for a way before that at that time to try to prevent the threats come true in some way, threats coming from SDS. We failed to convince them that there were not 7,000 rifles in Kozarac. They did not want to talk about it any more. They said that was that. Then we tried to suggest that in those places where they thought the Serb population might be in a precarious situation or that the installations used by the army might be endangered that we should set up a joint unit so that the Territorial Defence, police and the army and then that these joints forces should control the road through Kozarac and the road leading out of Kozarac along the Banja Luka/Prijedor exits, and in other places where they thought that the Serb population was apprehensive, but they refused even to think about it. They refused it automatically. They said: "Give back the weapons. There is no further discussion without that". In the end Mr. Medunjanin said, " Gentlemen, how do you think we can return 7,000 rifles when there are not so many of them?" and they told us, "That is your problem."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In addition to emphasising the strength of the Serbian military forces, did Zeljaja indicate specifically what he would do with those forces if the ultimatum was not met?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He said that, "Unless the Serb flag is in Kozarac and the Serb police in Kozarac, I shall raise Kozarac to the ground". That was towards the end of the meeting and he repeated it three times, and we understood everything then. At a certain point, I really felt very bad and I stood up to ask for a glass of water from a former colleague with whom I used to have drinks often before that, from Dragan Kurnoga, and Simo Miskovic was telephoning at the time, and I noticed an interesting detail which confirmed that they would not renounce their intentions, only they would try to use force. A telefax had just arrived and the girl who worked there was showing it to Miskovic. I was about a metre away from them, and I saw it was a list of medicines. They were listed one, two, three, about 25 medicines, I think, with those medical expressions, and in the end there was bandages. He told her to, told her to telephone immediately and to send a fax because they were requesting much more and what had been sent was too little. He said,"We shall need much more of this; fax it". I returned, sat down, and at the end, toward the very end of the meeting, Mr. Medunjanin said, "Right, I shall inform of your position the people in Kozarac and the people will decide whether they will accept the Serb flag and the Serb police, as you said. All I can do is guarantee that the Bosniak Muslims will not provoke you into any action, that you have no reason to fear anything, and that we are open for any kind of understanding". That was the end of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Semenovic, the telefax that you saw with a list of medicines and bandages, were you able to see where that was from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, I was not. It was too far away, I could not see that, but the lady or the young lady who operated the telefax and telephone had said that, "There is a telefax from Belgrade". She repeated it, "A telefax has arrived from Belgrade". During this brief discussion as I was waiting for Dragan to pour water for me, waiting for it, I heard that, and I was slightly surprised why medicine from Belgrade. I was not quite sure, but I knew that there was a major shortage of medicines throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina. It had lasted for several months already because of some measures of the federal government, medicines had to be paid for.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You mentioned the rejection by Serbian officials of the proposal that joint patrols be formed in order to reduce possible incidents. Do you know whether or not some joint patrols were formed, nevertheless?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Joint patrols were formed before that. It was our proposal and we fought for its implementation for about a month, as a matter of fact, for two or three months; in some places we managed to do that, in some local communes, and some Serbs, some Serbs admitted to us that they had to withdraw from those joint patrols because the party authorities, SDS, threatened them and were telling them that there was no need for this, that everyone should defend one's own. After that meeting there was no more communication between SDS and SDA. It was simply impossible to form any joint patrols.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Semenovic, about this time when Commander Zeljaja was threatening to raise Kozarac to the ground unless it turned over weapons it did not have, did Muslim leaders in the Muslim community begin to fear that, indeed, an attack was imminent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did the Muslim community have an organised armed force at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you make attempts to make preparations for the attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had a week at our disposal. Everything was clear, crystal clear. Our possibilities were very scarce and what we tried to do, the only way to do it was to organise it through lawful, through legitimate agencies which existed in peace time, such as Territorial Defence Reserve police force, and a smaller number of policemen who were expelled by the Serb authorities when they took over the power. They were lawful, legitimate agencies and the only way was to try to expand, to build the Territorial Defence in Kozarac, to bring in as many people as possible and organise some kind of defence if the Serbs really decided to use the armed force that was available to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was this to organise under the provisions of existing law within the Bosnia-Herzegovina structure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, exclusively under the existing laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did local communes then make an attempt to prepare some list of available men who could serve in such an organised force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How was that done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence Commander had lists of members of the Territorial Defence but that was a symbolic number of people, so it had to be extended. Then the local authorities met and it was agreed that in the view of the extraordinary circumstances and this is how it should be done by law, to expand the Territorial Defence. But then the question of records arose, that is, the lists of citizens who were in local communes, as the lists of voters and other lists of the population censuses. Then the Territorial Defence headquarters in Kozarac used those lists and then extended them, but it had to be checked of course in the field, because there was no coercion, there was no compulsion. The only principle was the principle of voluntariness. Then young people, who had enough time and who could go from one house to another, were sent out with those lists, and people who would agree to join the Territorial Defence had to sign their name. If they had any weapons, they were also requested to indicate what kind of weapons they had and if they had received it from someone. It was distributed on the basis of TO orders in an area, that is, even those weapons they were given by somebody should also register. A few days before the war in all the local communes where it was possible, there were people who went from one household to another and making this census and so that is how the list was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So because there was no organised military force it was necessary to first put a list together from census records and voter registration lists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As well as existing TO records which included some names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Approximately when was that list prepared and sent to the TO in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not know exactly because I did not take part in this directly, but I know when I signed my name on the list. I put my signature about four or five days before the attack organised by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I have exhibit D6? (Exhibit D6 handed to the witness). Mr. Semenovic, can you look through that document quickly and browse it and then, in particular, turn to page A1/7?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A1/7. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, do you recognise what this document is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These are the lists that our guys took around, took out from one household to another and, for those accepting it, to sign it and if they had weapons then also to put them on record and here is my name, 106, and I remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can I ask you to turn also to page A1/92?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: To assist the court, I know this can also be seen on the computer monitor, if your Honours do not actually have the exhibit in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We are proposing to do that right now with the assistance of Miss Sutherland. Can you put A1/92, yes, thank you. (To the witness): Mr. Semenovic, do you recognise these documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Yes, I can. These are summonses prepared on the basis of those lists in the Territorial Defence headquarters in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is that a summons pursuant to the existing law of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can I ask you to turn back to page A1/7 once more and is that your name that appears at No. 106?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is the signature you referred to earlier that you made about three days before the Serbian attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was the intended organised defence force able to be formed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To begin with, there were not enough weapons for any organisation, for any proper organisation, because the territory of Kozarac is very large, and there were no trained qualified people who could organise it properly. There were only three or four persons who did have some kind of military knowledge. All the others were ordinary people, civilians, and it had to be done with very, very few weapons and in a matter of only a few days in order to oppose, to stand up to, the force with inconceivable military potential already deployed around. A large part of the weapons that appears here on the lists was done manually, or there were some pistols of the Turkish times or hunting rifles. For instance, I remember that in the vicinity of the house where I lived in, at several sentry posts towards the railway tracks and fish farms, that was the direction from which we expected the infantry attack might be launched, the sentries were lads, were young men, who were not armed with anything. They did not have any rifles, most of them, not even those pistols, but they would have a bottle of petrol with a rag in, with a piece of cloth in it, and that was the only thing they had with them to spend on duty, to spend on guard thought the night. They did not know even how to make that, what you call it, Molotov cocktail. They simply poured the petrol from the car into bottles and that was how they did it. There was simply no time, no weaponry, nor skilled people, professionals, army officers, who could organise it, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would like to ask us to look at some of these entries. Going back once again to page A1/7. The information contained here are the names of the people who were approached and any weapons they might possess?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, every man on this list was approached in person, that is, they went to their homes and they signed this of their own will, of course if they wanted to do it. We see here that two did not want to sign that. Very many signed it even if they did not have any weapons. All those who did have a weapon indicated it here, any kind of a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What kind of weapons are listed on the page which you signed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Under 74, it says pistol, it is a revolver. Then there are two hunting rifles, an automatic rifle, a pistol, pistol, carabine and a hunting rifle, pistol, pistol 7.65 and others, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Turning to page A1/5, looking at the top of the page and to the right of the page, does that indicate your local commune?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I see that one, several of the listings, in fact, say "M48", what kind of a weapon was an M48?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a weapon. Yesterday you also asked me a question about weapons, a weapon of the Territorial Defence which had been removed and then a symbolic quantity of it was returned to the local communes. The majority of rifles returned to the local commune from the central depot which the army allowed to return were M48 rifles. They are rifles of World War II. They are not semi-automatic or automatic, slightly longer barrel, they do have two charges for every bullet you want to use. At present, it is a primitive and obsolescent model of weapon and it is not used anywhere. That was the principal kind of armament of the TO's. Most of the weaponry the TO had were M48s and a few automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The M48, is that an old bolt action World War II rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: For example, the name that appears between 22 and 24 -- it seems to be obscured on the screen -- there is an M48 listed in parenthesis, it says "TO-MZ", does that mean the Territorial Defence of the Mjesna Zajednica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes. Mr. Sivac, Vasif Sivac, is a gentleman who lived downstairs and he was a TO member and he had received weapons and he had this M48. The same is for those under 25 and 26, and they were all issued M48 in Trnopolje local commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So, in your local commune, at least in this list, there appear to be 106 men within appropriate ages to be placed on the list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that is where the Trnopolje local commune ends and where Kala (which is a suburban settlement) begins. In Kozarac, yes, we had 106.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Looking at the list, is it fair to say that there are fewer than 30 weapons available to those men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, and if we add up the weapons from Turkish type pistols and M48s, when we add them up all, that is then so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The majority of those 30 are pistols?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The rest is primarily comprised of hunting rifles and the M48s you have told us about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were there some communes which were even more poorly equipped? Let me repeat that question. We did not hear the answer. Were there some communes which were even more poorly equipped than Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There were local communes which were even more poorly equipped. I cannot tell you like this offhand because I was not directly involved in that, but I know that some local communes would borrow from others, because in some local communes there was absolutely no weapons, or one or two rifles, and in others there would be some 20 or 30 weapons of all kinds. So, it had to be distributed evenly. That is what the command of the TO did. That was their job.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can you turn to page A1/61, please, may that be displayed on the monitor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Does not all this speak for itself? If you want details, you should have it translated, the weapons, but that is the only thing that is not completely clear, is it not? We can understand "pistole". But if you really want details of all the weapons, then have it translated but, surely, you do not need to take this witness through it all?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I agree, your Honour. I had no intention of taking him through anything more than that one reference, and it appears that is unnecessary.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I had a question regarding communes. What is the commune, Mr. Semenovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A local commune is the basic territorial unit. Basic territorial unit is called a local commune. Local communes, several local communes form a municipality and several municipalities comprise a Republic, become a republic. It is a local government unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I noticed from this Exhibit Defence 6 that there appears to be more than one commune in Trnopolje. You are listed as in the Cesta, is it, C-E-S-T-A, Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Each local commune -- there is just one local commune, Trnopolje, but it was made out of several villages, that is, several parts. In the local commune, this is the administrative way of organising it, for various purposes, elections or other kinds of planning or building. So that is why there are parts of a particular local commune and Cesta was one part, there were also parts like Trnjani, Kararici and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were the communes composed only of persons of the Islam religion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, the local commune, Trnopolje, was comprised of 40 nationalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So that, for example, Trnopolje Cesta, which was one of the communes in Trnopolje, would be or could be, at least, composed of persons of different religions, Muslim ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- orthodox? How many communes were there in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Trnopolje is one local commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, but you have Trnopolje Cesta, you have Trnopolje Elezi, E-L-E-Z-I?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These are parts of the local commune of Trnopolje. It is always the local commune Trnopolje, but one part of it is called Cesta or Elezi or Hodzici or Matrici, it is parts of it. There is also a part call Redzici, part of the local commune of Trnopolje, or Garibi and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: On what basis then are these parts created?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They existed previously, since the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How many different parts then would you have of the commune, the Trnopolje commune, at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Within the local commune of Trnopolje at that moment there were just as before. I have mentioned most parts just now. I can make a full list of it, if necessary. It is something that is not changed. It is, for example, like streets within a city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Following up on the last question, are these parts of the commune multi-ethnic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. (To the witness): Where did the first military attack occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean in Kozarac or in general in the municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I am sorry, thank you -- in the municipality overall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first attack occurred in the evening hours of 22nd May somewhere around Hambarine, between Prijedor and Hambarine. We learned that through news on the radio and through those talky-walky machines (as they call them) that existed in the local commune and in the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did that occur after an ultimatum had been made to the people of Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, several days after the ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What happened the day after the attack in Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The following day, that part of the municipality was shelled, the village of Hambarine and also a part that was going from Hambarine towards Prijedor. It was a pretty heavy shelling. We could hear it, some kind of like some kind of a thunder, because from Trnopolje it is quite far away, some 10 or 11 kilometres from us. We noticed that after that shelling all the villages on the shelled part had been burned down. We could see enormous flames and smoke. We could see it quite clearly. We also heard explosions when they would fire the mortars and the explosion of the shelling. We could, as far as it was possible from a distance of some 10 kilometres, we could conclude that the shelling was done from the area of the Urije airfield or from the village of Cejrici, because we knew from beforehand that some artillery units had been located there but we could see very clearly where the shells fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How long after that was it that Kozarac was attacked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A day later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Had there been any reports to leaders of the Muslim community about troop movements or suspicious activity before that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some kind of a communication with this signalling equipment existed between the local commune of Kozarac and its Territorial Defence and the Reserve, militia Reservist and the Serb army in Prijedor. In local communes, we would receive just oral information when somebody would come and report on what was going on. I know they would communicate. They gave from Prijedor to Kozarac a clear cut ultimatum of a military kind, but I was not there. The talks were led by the chief of the militia -- police Reservists. His name was Osman -- I cannot remember his last name now -- and Becir Medunjanin, and I think they sent some people even then to try to negotiate. The chief of the police and other men were there and they did not come back. At the same time the army started to broadcast the ultimatum to Kozarac on the radio, to Kozarac and the extremists, to surrender arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I am sorry, Mr. Semenovic, let me try to get the chronology straight. Was the time period you were just talking about when communications were occurring and there was an attempt to negotiate before or after the attack began?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the attack on Hambarine and before the attack on Kozarac. The chief of the police from Prijedor was telephoning the chief of the police in Kozarac. The officers were calling the local commune in Kozarac also on the phone, and then they said they should return, surrender, their weapons within a couple of hours. I do not know exactly when because I was not there. I was at Trnopolje. From time to time, I would go to Kozarac and then go back home while that was still possible, only on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You mentioned in connection with the takeover that people in Serbian neighbourhoods had left their homes, come back, left their homes and come back a few times before the takeover actually occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was there any unusual movement by Serbian civilians prior to the attack in the Kozarac area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, even a couple of days before the attack, the Serbs from parts of the local commune of Trnopolje where they represented a majority, they completely withdrew and sent somewhere women, children and elderly people, only men remained in their homes. I cannot tell you where they sent them, but I heard they were sent across the fish farm towards Rakelici, a Serb village, and towards Omarska. I cannot tell you exactly where, but I know they were not in their homes any more. I am sorry, but I have to say to the Trial Chamber in order to clarify things, we were speaking about the multi-ethnicity of the local commune. In all parts the population was -- there were 14 nationalities exactly in the local commune. Most of them were Bosniak Muslims in the parts where these lists were made, but there were also Croats there, Russians, Germans, Ukrainians, Ruthenians, Czechs, Byelo Russians, Albanians, Romes, Turks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When did the attack actually begin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 24th, I think, in the early hours of the afternoon, somewhere towards noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where were you when it started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What did you do after the attack began?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I tried to go to Kozarac in order to receive instructions from the Territorial Defence to tell us what to do, because the Serbs were broadcasting on the radio that the army was going from the -- on the line Prijedor/Omarska across Trnopolje. It also received oral information that the army was going from on the road Prijedor/Banja Luka, going past Kozarac and that it was quite a strong military force moving. During the night, part of the Serb infantry entered Trnopolje and they were located around some Serb houses and we could see that during the night. When the shelling started, chaos started as well. I tried to go to Kozarac to try to see how to co-ordinate that and what we could do because we received information that we should let the army go by on one road because it was impossible for us to defend ourselves on both roads and, apart from that, I thought that the Territorial Defence did not have enough information on what was going on in Trnopolje. I went there by bike because it is a distance of four-and-a-half to five kilometres and I arrived to some 500 metres away from Kozarac, and I could not continue because the shelling was very intense and continuous. The explosions were awful, very strong calibre weapons, and the shells were falling all over. They were not particularly targeting. I waited there for sometime for them to stop and then to try and seize the opportunity to go through there, but for hours it did not stop, so I went back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You served in an artillery unit when you were in the JNA. Were you able to determine where the shells were coming from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They were coming from the direction of Omarska and the explosions -- one could hear the explosions for a long time. It came from the direction of Kozara, roughly speaking, the central part of Kozara around Mrakovica. It also came from Prijedor, from the direction of Urije, and the mortar fire came from the direction of Orlovci. Those were not cannons but mortars. They were a short distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: May we have Exhibit 79, please? (Exhibit 79 was handed to the witness) Mr. Semenovic, using A79, if it is possible, when it is pulled back or focused in, can you point out the places from where the shells were being fired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the monitor or? From the direction of Omarska, this is this direction here. This was from one side. The other direction it came from was Kozara, but the distance, well, it is much longer than represented on the map. Then from the direction of the Urije airfield, that is, to the north west of the town, roughly speaking here. And from here, from this part, we could hear mortar shells, between Garevci and Orlovci, somewhere in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How intensive was the shelling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the shelling was continuous. Very often at the same time a few shells would fall because they were firing from various areas at the same time. From the direction of Tomasica, there were also two shells that fell on the very village of Trnopolje, but from Tomasica they did not shell Kozarac. Those two shells, they were probably measuring the distance in - - I suppose that the mosques served as a bearing to them because the first shell fell some 500 metres in front of the mosque and the other one fell behind the mosque. At that occasion one person was killed and several were wounded. When the shell fell behind the mosque, it was some 400 metres behind it. So I think there was simply measuring the distance, as the military say. That particular artillery battery did not fire any more; whereas all the others were used all day long up until the next day. The following day, there were some intermissions and some appeals on the radio saying that the population could go towards Trnopolje in safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was there movement by parts of the population, or some portion of the population, toward Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the following day. On that particular day it was not possible. Those who managed to go to the shelter did that. People made very few shelters. They did not have time to do it. They were in the basements, and when the shellings stopped for the first time the Serb radio started with continued broadcasting, saying that the population could go to safe areas, and that was the area of Trnopolje. So, the people started from Kozarac to go to Trnopolje, and at the same time the people from Trnopolje went towards Kozarac in order to go to the Kozara mountain. These were huge columns. People were walking or using some vehicles or tractors, and those two columns met half way in between Kozarac and Trnopolje. Around the village of Hrnjici, between the village of Hrnjici and Gornji Sivci and Vutici. The roads were completely blocked. Nobody could go either in or out of Trnopolje. Various rumours were heard, so that most people in the columns spent the night there where they actually found themselves because it was impossible to go with the vehicles either back or forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you see what happened to any of the villages in the area, any specific villages in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Already on the third night part of the people left and went to Trnopolje. Some houses had already been burned down. They were put on fire, and from the direction of Petrov Gaj, there was very heavy firing, very heavy shooting, towards the parts where non-Serb population lived. They were also shooting on the people, on the refugees, with some Tromblon mines, guns, that are used for short distances. When the first larger group went towards Trnopolje, the Serb army appeared and they put all those people into camps. That was the day when that camp was opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you see what happened to Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the second night when the artillery fire had stopped for the first time, it was interrupted for some four hours, for some three or four hours, in the evening. Then we noticed that houses were on fire, houses that were at the beginning of Kozarusa and throughout the way to Kozarac. Around 11 o'clock in the evening, it was awful, the sight. All the houses were on fire. The flames were enormous. One could not really hear very much, very much the shooting, but some people who managed to run away from the shelters, they told us that the Serb infantry came and they were putting houses on fire one by one. They were doing it with some kind of grenades which were efficient because every house would burn in a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can you show us where Kozarusa is on the map in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the west of Kozarac. This is a suburban area of Kozarac. This is called -- what I could see, this whole part was burning from the road a couple of hundred metres away. There was all the houses there. It was an awful sight, a very apocalyptic. In theory, one could not even imagine so much fire and we could see it with our own eyes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I have one question or two questions, Mr. Tieger. Excuse me. (To the witness): Mr. Semenovic, you said a few moments ago that the Serb army appeared and they put all of those people in camps. You also a few minutes ago referred to the Serb infantry. By that, do you mean JNA troops or other Serbian troops?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were not called the JNA any more. At the last meeting of which I spoke sometime ago, they were called the Serb army, they said, "We are the Serb army." Officially, they claim they were the Serb Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they wanted their share. I have to say something else to you. What they formed in Trnopolje straightaway when they arrived, that camp, they did not call it a "camp". They called that "centre", a "reception centre" and they called all the population those they that said, quote, unquote, which did not have "blood on their hands", they said that they could come freely to Trnopolje. That centre, reception centre, was formed for innocent people in Trnopolje and they would be there safe up until the capturing of the extremists would have been finished, and after that each and every one could go home. They kept repeating that. A large number of people, unfortunately, believed in those words.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess for 20 minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. (To the witness): Mr. Semenovic, can you show us on the map where you hid over the days following the attack? Mr. Semenovic, you will have to wait until you return to your chair near the microphone before you can speak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the area between Trnopolje and Kozarac, the old road in the area of the village Gornji Sivci. That is several hamlets I mean together. This is in Gornji Sivci, Hrnjici, Gutici, Mujkanovici and Kenjari or, more precisely, this is the area around the Ukrainian church. It is this part here above the village of Sivci. This is where I spent most of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you spend some portion of that time in a converted septic tank and then move into the house of a woman who sheltered you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was her family reluctant to shelter you because of your political prominence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was very dangerous because the Serbs told the Muslims that they had to surrender their extremists and that anyone who had any connection with the alleged extremists, that is, SDA people, that any such person will be shot, and it was dangerous even to meet anyone of these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: During the time that you hid in the Sivci area, did Serbian troops come into that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, several times. To be more accurate, this woman's house, the house of the woman who hid me is not in a Muslim village. There are Ukrainian houses around it or galijani, as we call them. In the early days they were mobilized for the Serb army, but they were told to be on duty around their houses with their weapons and ammunition. I was in the house which was the only Muslim house in that place, and that is why it was safer than other houses. On several occasions, the Serb army passed through the area. I watched five operations of that kind. Every -- they, to use their term, ethnically cleansed every individual village, and since this part is on a triple boundary, that is, at a junction, they helped us to that area, that is, when they were cleansing Hrnjici, they also passed through Gornji Sivci, Mrkanovici, the same thing. The village Sivci, that cleansed on two occasions. They also got to this part. Sometimes I could see it very clearly, sometimes from the immediate vicinity, 10 metres or so away, the soldiers passing by, taking away groups of men, harassing them, firing shots and, invariably, after every operation they would leave a few dead people behind them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How were the cleansing actions conducted? What would the troops do first when they entered the area and how would they cleanse the people from the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First, they would encircle villages and a number of soldiers would be employed around the village from all sides. Then powerful fire simultaneously would take place and then the infantry would enter the villages. These villages had people who were completely unarmed, and then they would take men out of the houses, group them at individual points and if somebody would try to escape or resist them, they would shoot them. Then a bus would turn up after a very short while, or some other vehicle, and those groups were taken in the direction of Trnopolje at times and at times in the direction of Omarska. I did not know where they were taking them in the beginning; I learned that later. It also happened that there would be more people than could be accommodated in one bus or a vehicle, and then they would force some of them to move on foot towards Trnopolje or Omarska. After several such visits, there were no men in the villages any more, only women and children remained behind, and sometimes not even women or children. Every time, invariably, somebody would be killed in every passage. If they would not kill somebody in their house, then they would get two or three friends and kill them individually in the street. Very often, there are old men in the village, Gutici. They found a woman who was not a Muslim by origin. I think she was a teacher. She is Ukrainian. She was in her garden and, presumably, did not think it was dangerous for her because they were conducting their operations against the Muslims, but she was shot as she was in the garden, gardening there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: During the cleansing operations, how were the men who were taken from the houses and then taken away treated after they were collected from the houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They beat them in all the ways imaginable. They forced them to sing, to sing Serb songs. Those who did not know it were beaten. Once I was hidden in a boundary next to the road and I watched a whole group. An elderly man would fall down under the blows. They would put them up and continue to beat them, or they would stop them all and order them to sing in a choir, and people would not know the lyrics and then they would force somebody who did know the lyrics to start and all the others had to join in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What nationality were the soldiers who came in to conduct these cleansing operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serbs exclusively, only Serbs. Some of them were people, known people, that is, those who lived in Trnopolje or Prijedor, and there were those who were not known. They were mostly younger. At some point I could hear the conversation of a group of soldiers after the completion of cleansing. They started off towards Kozarac, and from time to time they would fire at a house, and they engaged in a private conversation, a group of seven or eight soldiers. Some of them were uniformed completely, some of them wore jeans and a military shirt above it. Some were younger, some were older. I recognised one of those younger ones as coming from Banja Luka because I heard him say to another soldier, they talked as they walked along, he said, "It pays this offer better than if I worked because this here is as if I had worked for a month in Banja Luka, I cannot buy anything for the salary I get", and I realised they must have been hard for a few days to do what they did. I heard some of them, two of them, I heard talking in an accent which does not come from the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I guess these were young soldiers, that is, young recruits from Serbia because that is how their pronunciation sounded like. Also, on another occasion when they were cleansing the village of Mujkanovici and Kenjari, I saw a group of soldiers who called themselves Vukovarians. That was, presumably, a unit which had come back from Vukovar and was conducting operations in the territory of Prijedor, and when they finished their business they drove in an APC towards Kozarac. There was a big Serb flag on the APC and a number of them were sitting on the APC. It was moving at a moderate speed and others walked behind them and they were moving towards Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you see any insignias on the uniforms of any of these soldiers or paramilitary troops?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They varied. There were some without any insignias. Some had insignia of the Serb army, some had insignia which I do not really distinguish them. Those from Vukovar had insignia of the so-called Marticeva militia, that is, army. There were all sorts of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Approximately how long did you continue to hide in the area you showed us earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until about 10th or 12th July -- just a moment, no, I am sorry, until I think 18th July, the second half of July. After all these cleansing waves, they literally cleansed everything, women, children, old folk. There was no-one in the houses any more. Then they systematically looted, plundered. They came for days on end. They had some points where they brought together the looted things. At first they did it rather calculatedly, and they piled up everything as it arrived. Later on groups of soldiers were placed in charge of various things. Some were collecting, amassing only the cattle; others were responsible for refrigerators, a third group for cooking stoves and as a fourth, and the vehicles came regularly sometimes every 12 hours or every 24 hours to take away all these things from those points, and coming out to the road between Banja Luka Prijedor. I do not know where they went on from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: After you left that area, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I started off towards Trnopolje as I intended to cross the fish farm and move towards Grmec. Since I was all alone, I did not want anyone to suffer because he had been supporting me. It took me some 10 hours to reach a place above the camp at Trnopolje, that is, some 500 metres as the crow flies, and I could -- I was higher up so I could watch all this that was below.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can you show us on the map, please, where that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Below the village of Cuskic towards the old road, this part here, roughly. It is a small vantage point, a hillock from which one can clearly see towards the station and this part here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What did you do after you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the first time I saw the camp. I did not hear anything because it was too far away, but I could see everything clearly. So I watched the whole area for two days and two nights because I had somehow to break through towards the fish farm. That place where I was is about 200 metres from the road, and I noticed that down the road came bus loads of civilians. So I came closer to the road through the maize field to see what were those vans, and in those buses there were men with their hands behind their heads and women and children in separate vehicles. It went on for a day, as far as I could see. Then the next day I saw a number of empty buses and trailers. I saw some of them move towards Kozarac and I guessed that it was the evacuation. The location was talked about while people were still in the field and I maintained contact with them so I heard that. They were saying that some individuals who were not responsible, who were not to blame for anything, whose hands were not bloody, would be transferred to the "free territory", in inverted commas, that is, the territory controlled by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So I thought that that was the beginning of that stage and that it was the evacuation. But it was too far away, and watching the area I realised that I could come closer to the camp to some 70 metres, that is, that I could come closer unobserved. I saw the guards. I saw the sentries. I knew their periods of time. I decided to approach it because there are acacia trees there, acacia groves and haystacks, and I thought I could approach enough to see what was happening inside, whether those people were being evacuated, whether they were distributed there, whether there were guards or sentries on duty. I did manage to do it the next night, that is, on the third night I managed to come close sometime before the dawn, sometimes crawling, sometimes moving normally but I came to about 70 metres from the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you observe the camp from there or decide to enter it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I observed it for about an hour, and I could see that complete chaos rained inside, thousands of men, women, children. I saw some of them carrying bags. I saw some of them packing. I saw a number of empty vehicles. I thought that I could come up to the wire. There was a safe way of approaching the wire and that if possibly I could manage there, because I saw some people next to the wire that I might ask someone and ask what was going on there. Only a deep trench, there was a channel there between me and the camp. On one side was maize, on the other side was wheat and they were separated. So I crawled through that ditch and blackberries were growing there, blackberry bushes. So I hid in those blackberry bushes, and I saw that the area in front of me people were using as a toilet, and I saw some men doing it there, that is, using it and I thought that I could crawl up to that and I could enter. I did recognise some faces, some of my friends, and I entered or, rather, took off the trousers, jumped on that levy and was squatted for about five minutes and then joined the others, and that was that, and that was when I met some of my friends immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Why did you want to get into Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wanted to get in there to see with my own eyes whether they were evacuating the camp or not, in case they were evacuating it. I thought that there were greater chances of my own survival if I had managed to join the convoy, that is, board the bus rather than move towards Grmec because it is 50 kilometres, no food, no water on the way. I also thought that if I would not be able to do that, that I would also be able to leave if I failed to board one of the buses, of course, at night-time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You indicated you met some friends shortly after you entered. What were their names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Adem Trnjanin, Asmir Trnjanin, Husein Trnjanin, they were my neighbours and friends, Ajdin Zenkic -- there were very many of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, did you ask them how the camp operated and seek information to allow you to fit in anonymously?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes, that was my first question. I could not get out as easily in day time because I saw machine gun nests in several places. I had known that beforehand, but they were so strong, there were so many soldiers around. But I was told that there were several thousand people inside and that I could hide there therefore, and there was a chance that they would all be evacuated because Slobodan Kuruzovic, who was the camp Commander, said that they expected to transfer all those people somewhere towards Gracanica any day now. They told me to be good to hide and then seize the opportunity, and they directed me to a place where I could hide. They also told me that they stopped calling out my name some month before that, because in the beginning Serbs used to line up all the men and then call out names. My name was one of those called out, Semenovic, but then they allegedly recognised my dead body somewhere in Kozarac and stopped calling me out. They stopped looking out for me. They had written me off. And they said that was another reason why I could hide there, stay there for a day or two and then be evacuated together with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you stay in Trnopolje for some days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At some point did you meet some friends named Foric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was the third or fourth night. For three days and three nights I was with a group of people who did not know me, who could not recognise me, and I gave a false name. I said I was from Puharska and not to scare them because of my political activities. On the third day some of them recognised me. On that day, that group of Foric, rather, of relations Foric -- they were all families from two or three brothers -- a Serb neighbour of theirs came to them and greeted them. He simply approached them and I was there. I turned my back on them, but I listened to the whole conversation and he told them, "Well, what about you, lads? What is new? When shall we play ball again?" because they were neighbours and they played ball together on weekends and after that he left. The next evening the Serb police came, a policeman in a blue uniform, and I observed it from some three or four metres. One of these Foric's, Zilo Foric, with whom I had struck friendship with in the meantime because I told him who I was, so they called this Zilo Foric. They talked behind a parked tractor for some five or eight minutes, and then they sent him back and he called out all his relations, his brother and all the others to stand up, put on their shoes and follow him. Meanwhile, two soldiers, another policeman joined that first policeman and the four of them took the Forics in an unknown direction behind the building of the old cinema and after that, I do not know. I know we heard, well, there were shots all the time, but we were all afraid that they would be shot. Some perhaps 10 minutes later, we could distinguish six shots, that is, two long bursts preceded them, two full bursts and then six individual shots. We thought that, perhaps, they were shot. We, of course, hoped that was not the case, but the next morning the management of the camp sent some people to bury six bodies. On the basis of the description, we, the friends and relations, concluded, inferred, those were Foric’s because one of them had the typical workers overalls, blue overalls, he was a man of some 44; one had tennis shoes, sneakers; the third one had rather longish fair hair. So I thought that it was because of me. I tried to find a way to get out of the camp as quickly as possible. I wanted to escape that first night, but I had some qualms of conscience so I asked a man who was also a neighbour of Foric's: "Was I the reason for that?" He said, no, it had nothing to do with me; that the Serbs were not aware of my presence there; that it had been done by their neighbour probably as a tit-for-tat for some things or, perhaps, because he was on those lines on the first day, because he was across that line, because he was among those who had defended the Muslim population. But, regardless of that, I decided to leave and I managed to get out that night. I started about 1.30. I had about half an hour at my disposal because at 2 o'clock a moon came out and then it was impossible to move about. I left the camp at about quarter to 2 and I followed the same path that I came to -- I already described it -- and I went back to that place where I was before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you stay there for a period of time before returning to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, two days. Before I left and after the Foric's were shot, a friend of mine wanted to escape too, and he told me to be the first one. If I succeeded, then he would follow the next day and if that planned evacuation would take place, then he would try to get out and leave a message for me at a place. The next day I came to look for this message, but there was nothing and I felt that something was happening that was not planned. I decided to leave that place immediately and to start towards the fish farm and Grmec. That day I saw 12 empty buses approaching the camp and six trailers, that is, trucks with two trailers. They came empty and were parked around the camp. I thought that, perhaps, my friend was unwilling to take the risk, and that he wanted to board, perhaps, one of them. I thought that perhaps it would be a good thing for me to board one of them because of if I missed the chance it might become more difficult later on. In the same way in which I got into the camp, the trucks were arriving towards the evening in twilight and not leave, so that I tried to get in the same way that I did it the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What did you discover when you entered the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I entered the camp I met Adem Trnjanin, my neighbour and friend, he was beyond himself, he said: "Mevludin, it's finished. They learned that you were here. They called 15 of us, interrogated. Many of us were beaten and we were given 48 hours to say where you are and if we don't they will shoot us and that line is 48 hours." Now within 40 hours troops were supposed to come from Prijedor to sweep the area where they assumed I could be hiding. I thought what to do. I again had two possibilities: to try to escape once again and stay where I was, knowing of course what would happen and I did not think very much because on one side there was one life, on the other there were 15 of them. So I opted for the second possibility. I asked him to give me half an hour to think what to say, what would be my best answer. After those half hour I bid them goodbye. I left messages, if they survived to take them to my family. I turned to this lieutenant, Lieutenant Slavko, he was the head of those guards, of the camp security, and he left after half an hour and this Slavko came.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you taken to any other official in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I was taken from that area between the school building and the gym building. I was taken across the road towards a house where I saw some 10 soldiers. In the house there was their commanding office and the office of the commander of the camp, Slobodan Kuruzovic. When that man Slavko was taking me towards there, the soldier started running towards me. Two or three of them managed to hit me. At the same time Kuruzovic appeared and he said: Are we going to do it straightaway?" And he said, "No, there will be some information. Leave it for now." After that they let go and went further on and Slavko Kuruzovic took me into the room where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did they ask you questions in the room? How did they treat you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but they did not beat me there. They asked me a series of questions, but it seemed this was out of their personal curiosity: How did I manage to survive, where did I hide; how did I manage without food. One of those soldiers was rushing it all out, he said: "We have to go, we have to go", that is what he was repeating. I did not know what was going to happen. After about an hour, at some point I was taken out and in front of that building there was a green Mercedes and they put handcuffs on my arms. They put my hands behind the back first and then they handcuffed me, and they took me into the car. Slavko which I mentioned before was driving. Next to him was a vet technician, Branko from Kozarac, and he asked me for a couple of times: "Where's your friend? Where's your buddy?" and it was my friend Sead who had been killed and who used to be his boss at work. He was killed at Omarska. He asked me for a couple of times: "Where's your buddy? Where's your buddy? Where did you see him last?" He was laughing all the time. Next to me a soldier entered the car. He was a twin brother of that other twin brother who remained in Trnopolje. They started the car and we drove towards Prijedor on the old road. When we were passing by my house they were going, they were shooting: "Look over at your house" and so on. They were laughing, provoking. I could see on the journey burnt Muslim houses, bullets in the houses, every one was raised to the first floor level.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where were you finally taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To Prijedor. First of all, we stopped near Keraterm. On the opposite side there was a building that was used as a military prison. That is where we stopped. The driver, Slavko, and that other man, Brano, they left and went into that building. Some 15 minutes there was the soldier and myself who were there waiting. I could see across the road the camp Keraterm and I could see awful scenes. It is very difficult to describe them, skeletons. I did not talk to that soldier but at some point he asked me: "Mevludin, how come you were a deputy politician and you live in such a house?" I said: "That is how it is when you live honestly." As his question was not a provocation, that is what I thought at least, I thought maybe I could ask him something I was interested in and ask him: "Can you tell me whether they will kill me straightaway or later on? How do you do these things now?" and he said: "It does not mean that they will kill you. It all depends on what you will tell them." I was silent for some time and then I said: "What would be the best thing to say to them?" He said: "I do not know, Mevludin. I hope that Allah will help you". That is exactly what he told me. Then we stopped talking and very soon the other two came, and they took me to the Prijedor SUP, to the police station building.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Once you got to the SUP where were you taken and how were you treated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was taken to an office. Straight from the beginning a gentleman came in. His surname is Saponja. I think his name is Dragan Saponja. They started beating me right from the start. After that they started provoking. There was a man, somebody I knew, I drank coffee with him from time to time. He was a student of criminology. He did not complete his degree but he became an inspector. I was beaten in his office. I could bear that up until the moment when Saponja started hitting me over my head with a police rubber baton, and after the eighth blow I fell down and he made me stand up and took the belt from my trousers, put it around me and said that: "This is a tie for you". Then he took me to another room where there was an inspector and a policeman whose name I do not know but I remember him. He used to be a regular policeman before the war in Prijedor. At the same time they brought a shoe box and in there was a video tape, two of my diaries, an old one and a more recent one. There was a magazine there and these were to be the proofs against me. Then the first hearing had started.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was the magazine that was a proof against you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a theological magazine. My father was a priest. He received regularly a theological magazine. That was a magazine called the "Islamic Thought", Islamska Misad. One could regularly obtain it at news stands. The issue was four years old. They were probably not looking quite carefully. They could have found some more recent issues, but that had to be the proof for the accusations made later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you taken to a cell once they finished beating you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was there anything about the condition of that cell that indicated what had happened to prisoners who had been there before you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There was quite a lot of blood in the cell. On the walls there were bullet holes. On the right-hand wall above a metal bed some one metre above it there was an awful blood stain and a stain of brain. It was a bullet hole and then there was something like as if you took some mud, red in colour, and then smear it all around. It was an indication that somebody was shot at very close range there. They took me in and at that time there were two men and two women there in the cell. I remember that. I also remember that after an hour and a half there was a man who came near me, because they threw me on the floor in front of the cell. They also beat me so it was impossible for me to stand up. Those people tried to put me on a bed and I asked where they were coming from and they said they were from Cela which is a suburban area of Prijedor. They were simply taken from their houses and these two women were taken from the street where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you recognise the people who beat you in front of the cell? Were they police, soldiers, local people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, part of them were locals whom I could recognise. Part of these young men were unknown to me. They had slightly strange accents. I suppose these were men of the special units from Serbia, as they used to be called the Red Berets. I know they were some kind of emergency platoon, some kind of their best type of police. There was mistreatment, abuse, put a knife under your throat, beatings. They wanted to take me to the dormitory, but they did not do that because those from upstairs ordered not to transfer me there. But they would come from time to time, hit the metal door, kicked the metal door, and they said: "The MP will come to see you". At some stage two policemen came. They opened the door and I thought the same would be repeated again. Then the inspector asked me": "Can you tell me where the evidence is?" I said: "There aren't any more". He said: "This is nothing. We want real evidence." Because they accused me straightaway, they said: "You're a fundamentalist. You can claim that you are not, but we know that you are because your father was." I did not have any kind of other evidence and I proposed that they could go to my house, they could search everything, that I could go with them. There were dozens of other magazines like that. They closed the door and left. Then they took these other men and women out and I spent the night in the cell. The next morning they came to fetch me. They took me out of the cell, through the SUP building. I was tied with a belt and that is the way they took me around and they were saying" "Clear the way, we are taking the MP with us." The belt around my neck was very tight, they were pulling it. They took me to the bus parked there. I noticed women and younger girls that were going on the bus, they had makeup on them, and one or two soldiers would enter as well. At that moment Mr. Simo Miskovic entered into the SUP. I caught his eye and I expected him to look at me. I was hoping that maybe I could ask him a question, but he turned his head away and went by. Then we went on the bus and I was taken on the road Prijedor Kozarac to Omarska. We came to the Omarska settlement. So that is where I understood where I was going, but I could not understand why these women with makeup were going there and the civilians, but when we arrived there these were employees, they worked as secretaries there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: To what part of the camp were you taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, I was taken next to the administrative part. I was taken off the bus and passed near two groups of people who were sitting with their legs and arms pulled up and there were some kind of squares. The squares around him had metal chains, so that is how these were sort of squares. I was taken into this administrative building. We went up the stairs. There was a table there and a soldier was sitting there and next to him were other two soldiers. They took my name and then I was taken through this central part of the so-called pista towards a small white house that was at the end. They took me to the so-called white house. They took me there and left me there. The policemen who escorted me went out and for a minute or two I was there on my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Semenovic, looking at Exhibit 130 can you point out the white house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. This way came the bus. That is where I was taken to the first floor, and then here to the white house. They came in and took me to the first room on the left, this window on the left and that is where the soldiers came later on watching how they were beating me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What happened after you were placed in the first room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some two minutes later a civilian came in. One could see that he was a camp prisoner because everything was dirty what he was wearing. He came to me and said: "Were you an MP?" and I said, yes, and he started to beat me. He did not have any kind of a stick or anything like that. He was beating me with his hand. It lasted for some 10 minutes after which he went out. After that a Serb soldier came in and he started to beat me and these were quite heavy blows. On that occasion they fractured this bone here. Probably these first ribs were broken because it was very difficult for me to breathe and very painful. I could not open my mouth. After that second man a third man came in.
