The second one had some kind of a pole, a metal kind of pole, there was a yellow sort of transparent bit over it, it must have been some 70 or 80 centimetres long, and he was beating me with the pole. After that a third soldier came in and at the same time five or six soldiers were at the window. I could see their heads. They were watching it all, and they were saying: "Oh, is this the MP? He arrived just where he should be, excellent." After the fifth one who came in with the same mission I realised they were following a certain order because they could have entered, all of them, as in the prison in Prijedor but, no, they came in one by one. After the fifth soldier I was completely bloody because at some moment I fell and he hit me with his boot in my nose and face and within a couple of seconds I was completely in blood. An old man was taken in to clean my face. He did it and then I was taken out towards the policeman who first took me in towards the administrative building. Then the soldier started to run after me to beat me, but the policeman who was behind me told him: "We should not touch him during the interrogation. After all, we will all have our turn." This last I quoted. I realised what was going on but I was very scared because I heard that people for 10 days would be beaten and dying like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you taken in for interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was to the upper storey. Roughly speaking, somewhere in the middle of the corridor on the right-hand side there was a room. In every room I heard there were soldiers. I heard some screams from various rooms. I was taken into a room where a gentleman was whom I noticed on the bus when I was driving from Prijedor. He was some three seats in front of me and he was turning around. He was an elderly man and his name was Dragan Radakovic. He was seated at the desk and there were two Serb soldiers there very heavily built, and there were three of us in the room. I was told to sit down which I did. First of all, he asked me: "Did they beat you?" I was silent and he repeated his question once again in more severe tone. I said: "I don't know what is better to say, that they did or they did not", and he answered: "You can say they did because you are all in blood. It's one of your's who beat you, isn't it?"

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you agree with him that it was a Muslim or a Croat who had beaten you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I said yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did he ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, he asked me, I said: "Yes, that's correct", and he asked me: "Did anyone else beat you?" and I said I cannot remember because I lost consciousness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did he introduce himself to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that he introduced himself. He said: "My name is Dragan Radakovic. I am the manager of the National Park Kozara. We should have been colleagues because you are in the Managing Committee of the National Park as one of the MPs because the Parliament always had two members on the Board of each National Park". He said: "I am a sculptor and have an MA degree in psychology." Then he started to interrogate me and ask for information. When he started he said exactly the following: "We are not interested in Prijedor. We know that you did not have weapons. There were a few weapons but it's negligible. We are interested in Sarajevo. Sarajevo is our interest." He repeated that several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What nationality was Mr. Radakovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Radakovic is a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What nationality were the men who beat you in the white house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serbs. They were Serb soldiers except for that first man, a camp prisoner who was a Muslim, his nickname was Besa. That is what I remember. I think that his surname must have been Besic and that he came from a village above Kozarac but he used to live for quite a long time, I think somewhere in the area of Gornji Puharska and he was ----

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you know why he beat you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. I cannot remember the reason. He only did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was he a prisoner in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did he receive any special treatment or special favours from the camp guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How long did the interrogation conducted by Mr. Radakovic continue for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean that day or all in all?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All in all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For several days. I think for six days.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At the beginning did he concentrate on the area he mentioned at first, questions about Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, and almost all the first day he was interrogating me about two Serbs who remained in the Bosnian government. They refused to leave the Bosnian government and go to Pale. That was Mr. Zepinic and Mr. Simovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you beaten during the interrogations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. No, I tried to find a way to prevent it. I was aware of how things would go and at one moment when we remained just the two of us in those rooms, I told him a couple of sentences for which I think they had an impact on him. So he decided to prevent the beatings, at least for the next couple of days. I said exactly what follows: "Sir, we are alone now the two of us. I am 30 years old and I know that my life is at its end. You do this job" -- because he would constantly be saying, "I do this job, I am coming to this job" -- "So you do this job and it is your objective to do it as best you can." I told him: “ will sign whatever arranges you. You can freely write down that I killed 100 Serbs, that I managed to ensure two trailers of weapons, but while you and I are alone do not force me to lie, to tell things that are not true. While we discuss I will tell the truth, but we can have the following agreement. You will have an ideal report, you can just write it down and I will sign it without any problems, but I will ask you for a favour. While this lasts please spare me from beatings because I think they are not necessary. You will get whatever you want. You will realise what you have planned and after that let me die in a decent way, as a man should." I also said something that might have moved him. I told him that: "Somebody will survive this war. I have got two sisters, a mother and at least one of those three would survive and on the last day I will send you a message and I will ask you that one day when everything is over you give this message to one of my family, and they will really know how to be grateful to you because you spared their son and their brother from beatings." I told him all these things for two reasons: So that they would not force me to try and find that some people are guilty and give the names of some people who were at the camp, and in case I would tell them I did not know, so that they would believe me and, as much as I could, so that I could die in the least painful way. I think I did achieve some effect because he told me then he could not talk any more. So after some five minutes of silence and looking through the window I could not see his face then, he went to the door. He asked for the guards and he said: "Take him to the glass house", and I did not know what that meant before I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you taken to the glass house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we run the film, please?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What exhibit is this, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I am sorry, your Honour, this will be Exhibit 133 ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection to 133 or is it in? It is not in yet, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection to 133?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK, Exhibit 133 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Actually, your Honour, since we should watch it I would like it marked for identification first if that is possible, since we do not have it in front of us.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK, that is fine. How long is the film?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Very short your Honour. (The video was played).

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Semenovic, did you recognise the place depicted in that video?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. The way you showed it on the right-hand side of the glass house, whereas, the people who were filming were in the kitchen, the canteen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is that you sitting down who was in the close-up shot taken in that video?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I could recognise first myself. I was the first one next to the glass. I remember when the foreign journalists were filming that. That is the shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I have this marked as Exhibit 133?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Well, it is more appropriate to identify it first. So that is Exhibit 133, a film. In which camp was that, Mr. Tieger, or Mr. Semenovic? Is that Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That film was done in the Omarska camp somewhere early August, let us say 5th August, the 5th or 6th August. I cannot be sure, but roughly speaking around that time. These were foreign journalists. It all happened suddenly. One morning we noticed a great change in the Serb soldiers in the camp. They all wore very clean new uniforms. They all had new rifles and the difference from the previous days when the rifles were on their shoulders and that day they all had them in their hands, all of them really. We did not know what that meant, but sometime just before noon we noticed a larger group of journalists and some camera men. They came in and were filming all around. One of the cameras was near that glass, but I felt that I did not turn round, it might have been dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note that we marked 133 for identification. I would now tender it for admission.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 133 is admitted. It is very short. Could you play it again? (The video was played once more).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. We will stand in recess until 2.30. (2.30 p.m.) PRIVATE MR. SEMENOVIC, recalled Examined by Mr. Tieger, continued.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, would you like to continue, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. (To the witness): Mr. Semenovic, you indicated that you were held in the glass house in the administrative building of Omarska.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did people in the glass house receive treatment different from the other prisoners in Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, their position was somewhat better.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did people sometimes pay guards or bribe guards to get put in the glass house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, people could buy a place there. They paid in money or gold. At a point I saw Mr. Helmija Nukic. He probably had no more money and the last he had was, I think, a gold chain from his pocket and gave it to a young man who was there as a cook. Some other people I talked to, who did talk to me, they said they had arrived to the nursery, to the glass house, by paying a certain amount of money. In the beginning, those were considerable sums of money and then as the time went on, less and less. I also noticed that some people in the glass house were in a decent state, unlike other people whom I could see passing through to lunch running. Most of them were like skeletons. Some had their arms broken, some could not even move and were led by others. Some of them were transferred to the glass house. Others found a way to give to the Chetniks the money, as that was that they often called themselves and thus improve his condition. Among the people in the glass house, I noticed a gentleman who was a clerk in the SUP. He was completely blue from head to toe with enormous bruises, and I thought that he had been beaten in the “staklenik”, and then was told that he was transferred from some other room to the glass house the day before I arrived. They kept there a certain number of people who participated in the war on the side of JNA on the front in the Republic of Croatia, that is, those who served them as soldiers for a while and when they returned home they were also put in a camp in Omarska, but they were treated in a somewhat better manner, that is, they were put in the glass house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you protected from -----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Excuse me, I do not think you have pointed out where the glass house is on the plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. (To the witness): Mr. Semenovic, can you take the pointer and show us where the glass house is located, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The administrative building had two blocks. Those here were offices and they were used as offices where interrogations were conducted. Then there were some auxiliary buildings open on two sides. This side was hollow space, that is, open space. There was no roof there, and this is adjacent to the canteen, and it has glass all around. That is why they called it a glass house, that is, so a roofless part of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I noticed that there is a relatively good view of the building available on the monitor. If I might remove the roof, it might assist the court?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Regarding your request, Mr. Tieger, for a camera, I spoke with the director of our video operations. He said that he is going to mount a camera on the table so that it will focus down. He thought that would be a better view. That will be done next week, so I do not know what we will see now from the top, that is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the glass house, this is the canteen, that is the dining room, here is the door, the entrance, and the inmates used this entrance. They would pass this corridor here that I am showing now. Then to this line when they queued for food next to the door of the glass house, and this, and the door was, the door to the glass house was here, here in this part.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Semenovic. During the period of time you were in the glass house were you protected from being beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Soldiers attempted to enter the glass house several times, rather, to take me out, but they were forbidden to do that because the inspectors had planned photographs to be taken, rather, some footage, video footage, to be made there. For that reason, so I would not appear too deformed, I was beaten only on the first day and this footage that we saw today were made, I think, on the eighth day of my stay in the glass house.Then an inmate was also in the glass house who used to beat me, whose nickname was Besa. His cot was next to mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The man who was the first person to come in the white house when you first came to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Radakovic eventually prepare a statement for you to sign?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the minutes of the interrogation, as I was told, was to be signed after the completion of the procedure and in his office. I did not sign these minutes, but I was shown a statement a few days before that which I was to read before the cameras of the local television, to read it, literally looking at the camera and then answer and then read answers contained in the previous statement. I did that two or three days before this film was made, that is, before foreign journalists entered the camp. This interview was done by Mr. Mutic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Radakovic ask you about any other prisoners in the camp? Did he ask you about Anes Medunjanin, for example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Since the interrogation lasted several days, he used often to philosophize about life. He told me about various things concerning his profession and it was not conversation, it was more like a soliloquy and, of course, the position I was in I could only listen. He spoke about the very difficult position of Serbs in Tuzla and I am quoting now, "This is the hotel. This is how Serbs in Tuzla live. There Muslims draw water from briny wells, from brackish wells, and sprinkle the water in the state of Tuzla, and there the Serbs are standing in the sun for days on end and have to lick this brackish water off the grass, and they are even thirstier than before; how that is a terrible torture; and how one lives in Omarska where they get one meal daily and where they have water and how it is a genuine hotel when compared with Tuzla". He also indulged in some thoughts, theories, about life and then at a certain point asked me if I knew Anes Medunjanin. I said I knew his father who was one of the Party Executive and Anes is a youngish man. I knew him as a child but, objectively speaking, I could not socialise with him. Then, but came as a surprise, he said how he was a wonderful young man, how much that lad knew about the orthodox faith, that "I do not know about Islam as much as he knows about the orthodox faith, and perhaps he is more familiar with the orthodox faith more than I do. I could not really believe how such a fundamentalist, how such a Muslim extremist, could prove to be such a nice, bright young man", and then he told me, "I will acquaint you with Anes Medunjanin".

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you recall how many times you were interviewed by journalists in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Three times. The first and the second interviews followed each other. They were in the same room and at the same time. So, on the same day, one after the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I want to ask you about how you were finally able to leave Omarska. At some point were you taken from the glass house and to an office in the administration building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was a day after the arrival of foreign journalists, the day after the footage that we saw. When foreign journalists left, I was taken to the upper floor, to a large room in the central part of the administrative building on the left-hand side,and a television Pale team came there. They introduced me and they switched on their cameras and introduced me as an SDA official,a former member of parliament who came to Omarska of his own free will, to see how those people lived there. They said that they were unfairly accused of having a concentration camp and asked me to confirm that it was not a concentration camp. Then the next question was to ask, to tell them how the religious class, how the religious people were the first, were armed or, rather, how the clergy was armed first. They asked me to list responsible persons. I only gave the name of the first person of the party, Mirza Mujadzic, because I was certain he was in Bihac. For about a month before that, we had heard on a small transistor radio an interview that he gave to the local radio in Bihac. I did not give any other names. Then they left for Trnopolje and I was returned to the glass house. The next day in the morning the police came again. They took me to the same room again that I was in the day before, and some time later, perhaps after five minutes, a gentleman came in whose face I could remember at that time. I remembered his face but I could not remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did he introduce himself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he entered, offered to shake hands with me and said, "Do you remember me?" I then thought he was a gentleman from the municipal hall in Prijedor, a Serb. He looked like a gentleman whose name is Bereta and I said, "Yes, I remember you from the Assembly", and he said, "Yes, I am Vojo Kupresanin, President of the Autonomous region of Banja Luka. I remember you well from Sarajevo, from the Assembly", and then I realised who that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What else did Mr. Kupresanin tell you that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He sat next to me and started a political discussion with me, the discussion that I could not take part in; after all that had happened, I simply was unable to. It all seemed to me, it is a situation difficult to describe, death all around and at that moment somebody asks you about political views. I knew he dwelt at length before he asked any questions, that it was rather hard on the Muslims, all that was happening, that Europe has assigned to the Serbs the role of executioners of the Muslims. He said that it was a Vatican conspiracy and that the time had come to do something to improve the situation. He spoke, he went on, for about five minutes and then a soldier came in and called him and said, "Excuse me, Mr. Kupresanin, Mr. Karadzic needs you." He went out to the telephone. I could see that it was in the next room, the table diagonally across the room. I could see it and Kupresanin began to converse with Karadzic. What Karadzic asked him or told him, I do not know because I could not hear that, but I heard him repeating several times, "300 beds, we need 300 beds urgently. Send it, send them and send plenty of soap and detergents, if possible, during the day". Then he was silent for a while and then said, "I have found only one." I was not sure if he meant me by that, but I assumed that it was possible that he had meant me by that; who were the others, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did Kupresanin take you from Omarska and take you to members of your family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He took me out from Omarska. He was coming back towards the room where I was in and I thought he would continue the conversation, but he said, "You are coming with me." I did not know what that meant. I started, I asked the permission to take my jacket from the glass house and to say "goodbye" to those who were staying behind, wanted to let them know that I was leaving because I guessed I would probably not be coming back. So I went there. I took the jacket, said "goodbye" to people. I went out to the pista where two cars, two police cars, were parked. Kupresanin and I and his driver took one and the other one was boarded by policemen, so they put on those rotary lights and started, set off towards Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: On the way did he ask you where your family was and then did he take you there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he did. First, he asked me if I knew where other members of parliament from the municipality of Prijedor and Sanski Most were. He meant MPs, Bosniaks Muslims. He asked me where Mirsad Mujadzic and Rasem Cero;I said that Mr. Mujadzic was in Bihac and that Rasem Cero was in Sarajevo, that she had never returned. Then he told me: "You are going to Banja Luka. We shall take you to a Serb village. You will be in a house on your own. We shall bring you food. You have to get better. You have to recover. In about a month's time, we have to find your family". He asked: "Where are members of your family?" and I said that some of them with whom I lived, that is, my mother and my sisters,that they were already up road, and I lied about that, and I had heard messages on the radio, and I asked -- I was asked about the other sister. I had a sister in Bosanska Vrbanja who lived there before the war, and I thought that Vrbanja had suffered the fate of Kozarac. I said that she was up there, expecting to see his reaction, that is, his answer. Then he said, "If she was there before the war, then she is still there", so I asked if I could go and visit her, so that I could see that she was alive, and then possibly the International Red Cross should be notified about that. He said that they would take me to visit my sister. Now, it all happened while we were moving towards Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you learn at some point why Mr. Kupresanin was treating you so well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It became logical when we entered the building of the municipal hall. The car stopped in front of the building of the municipal hall. We entered, went upstairs to the left, somewhere towards the end of corridor, the office to the right. We entered it and that was his office. Around there there were some other offices, some had open -- doors open with tables in between and then again I could hear the conversation between him and Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So Mr. Kupresanin spoke with President Karadzic again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, and he insisted again on those beds, on those 300 beds, to be urgently sent and soap and detergents and he mentioned clothing, money, but I did not get that. I realised that later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How did you know that Mr. Kupresanin was speaking to President Karadzic on the other end of the phone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They talked about the same topic, and when the telephone rang the person who was there in the office who responded said, "President Karadzic needs you". But it is that black telephone, old model, so one could hear it. It is rather loud and I could hear Mr. Karadzic. Mr. Karadzic has a rather harsh voice. After all, I had listened to it for a year and a half during those long sessions in the Republican parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You mentioned something about clothes and indicated you ultimately realised you did not receive them. Why do you think Mr. Kupresanin was interested in getting you new clothes? What was intended for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know that at the time. I could infer it and I was not quite sure whether it concerned me, but about some half hour later some men entered the room, some army officers in uniform, some civilians. They questioned me about how about was it in the camp, what did you eat, were they taking people away. I mostly kept silent because I felt it was dangerous to say anything. At a different point in time a soldier with a long beard entered the room and asked at the door, "Where is he?" Then he entered the room and I was sitting in the chair like this. He went around me, encircled me, looking at me and repeating, "You were lucky, you were in luck, you were in luck". Then they took him away and later I learned that he was from Gradica and that he had taken part in those operations in Trnopolje. He was about 40 years of age, slim, a low height, and they took him away. Then Kupresanin said, "We shall take to Vrbanja now. We shall see what the situation is there. It might be dangerous for you to stay there". I may mention here that Vrbanja is ethnically homogenous, in that the central part is inhabited exclusively by Muslims Bosniaks. He told me that it was dangerous for me to go there because Vrbanja is full of fundamentalists, extremists. He asked me if my brother-in-law was an extremist. I said, "No", because he was never active in politics. He simply worked in a factory when he came back home and went fishing, and that was all. Kupresanin said then, "Well, now you will live like a man. We shall get some clothes for you. Now you must get fatter. In about a month, you must recover properly. We shall give you money". He asked me more seriously rather than jokingly whether I preferred dark girls to fair girls or vice versa. Then he said, "We will find you a girlfriend". About an hour later they said: "We will be off to Vrbanja now". So we set out to Vrbanja in a car. As we were approaching my sister's house, they said I was to go in first and just say that Mr. Kupresanin was there and his driver and some other army officers and they wanted to talk to them, to my sister and brother-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Semenovic, at some point did Mr. Kupresanin ask you to contact Muslim officials outside the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that happened a couple of days later. They came to fetch me by car and they took me to Banja Luka, to the town hall. He told me that they have been trying for a couple of days to contact Tuzla and Zenica, and that I had to try to telephone to Zenica. They told me they could not do it because whenever they telephone, Zenica puts the phone down and refuses to talk, and they had to talk to Tuzla something about electricity. They told me that I could and should do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you attempt to do so and were you successful?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not, I could not. Then they told me that I could call my friends in Sarajevo. All the telephone lines were cut, but they had the control and they could switch any line on. They told me that I could call to Sarajevo, Tuzla, Prijedor, Zenica. I was in a situation when I could not refuse everything they asked me to do. So I telephoned two people in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So you refused to call Tuzla and Zenica but agreed to call Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At some point did Mr. Kupresanin have you taken to the Skupstina opstina building, Municipal Assembly building, in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they came to Vrbanja on several occasions and took me there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was there one occasion on which you were taken for the purpose of meeting the President?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. One day they came and asked me to shave very quickly, within five minutes, then to take off a t-shirt where it was written "Levis America" and put something else on. They told me: "Now you are going to meet President Karadzic. He needs to talk to you about something". I supposed what it was all about because the previous day I heard on the radio that Lord Carrington and Cyrus Vance were coming to Banja Luka. They were on that particular day in Banja Luka, so I suppose that they would tell me that I have to tell those gentlemen something.I had no choice, so I went with them to Banja Luka.They took me to the Municipal Assembly building.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were there soldiers there when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, very many. The building was full, officers, soldiers, civilians, politicians, policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you see any politicians you knew from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw Mr. Srdjo Srdic and Mr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did either of them talk to you or did you overhear any conversations they were having?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were taking me up the stairs, I mean, Kupresanin and the police escort, and then up on the first floor it was very noisy. They were arguments. I could hear people swear. On the right-hand side, I saw Messrs. Stakic and Mr. Srdic. They were swearing at Karadzic's mother. They were mentioning some buses. Srdo Srdic was saying, "I have nothing to do with the buses. I do not want to know about anything on the Vlasic". At one moment he saw me with Kupresanin and some metres away he shouted towards me, "Mevludin", and he came towards me. He took me by my arm and took me to the group which was arguing there, most loudly and he told me, "Mevludin, tell me, has my foot ever been put into the reception centres at Keraterm, Trnopolje and Omarska?" Then he said, he turned towards them, "I do not want to be responsible for anything. I have nothing to do with the buses". I was quiet. It was a terrible feeling. I felt, as we say, as a sheep in front of many wolves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you hear any discussion about the removal of authority from the autonomous region or from any -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. These swear words against Karadzic, it was because they were trying to wash their hands of something, some buses.At that moment, I did not have any idea what buses they were thinking of. I suppose those might have been the buses that during the night were going from Omarska to the so-called exchanges, but they were not mentioning Omarska. They only mentioned the buses and Vlasic. They were swearing at Karadzic because he abolished autonomous regions. Mr. Srdic literally said, "He gave all the power to the Presidents of the Municipal Assemblies, to the Mayors; how come he has the right to do that? Now these Presidents of Municipal Assemblies do what whatever they want". He gave an example,that Stakic's people in the end burnt down the houses in the Muslim village of Gomjanica and that that had not been previously arranged. He said, "This is not the way to do our policy. What are we now going to show to the foreigners if they come?"

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Kupresanin ever ask you to assist him with negotiations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. One of the first things that he wanted to do was, they had to create some kind of a round table in Banja Luka. He said as follows: Bihac is going to be the part of the Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, of the Banja Luka region. A Muslim will be the President of the government, the Prime Minister. We have got a very excellent man, Fikret Abdic. We have already agreed with Fikret Abdic. He will be the Prime Minister and the Serb will be the President, and the Muslims in Bihac will be satisfied and all those Muslims that remained in Banja Luka as well. He said they were planning to organise a public panel transmitted on TV, and at that panel I should also take part at the panel as a representative of the Muslim people. I did not answer in either way, either "yes" or "no". I was, nevertheless, conscious that I should not go into something like that because I knew what the final issue should be. But, however, they did not tell me exactly what they were planning to do. I learned that from the Serb soldier who took me back to Vrbanja from the Municipal Assembly. He somewhere towards a third of our journey told me exactly like this: "It is very good that you had decided to become a member of the Serb assembly. I appreciate that, but it is very dangerous for you, and you have to be aware the Muslim extremists". He said that the pass that was made for me by Kupresanin and which would allow me to go through the Serb checkpoints, army checkpoints. He told me not to show it, that is, to make several photocopies of it, because otherwise they would make many -- they would tear up all, many of these photocopies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At some point did Mr. Kupresanin ask you go to Kotor Varos and talk the Bosnians into surrendering?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. One day he sent a gentleman who was Bosniak Muslim by nationality, a dentist from Banja Luka. He was more proYugoslav in his political opinion and he continued to co-operate with the Serb authority. He sent him to tell me that I had to go to Kotor Varos and to talk the Muslims into surrender,and that they should evacuate Kotor Varos. I could not accept that; I refused it. I said it would be much easier if they killed me in Vrbanja than to be killed in Kotor Varos and that I could not accept something of that kind, and I also said it, to my mind, that was, I could not help in any way by doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you refuse to go to Kotor Varos because you were afraid of being shot while you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. I refused. I gave them different reasons, different from my real reason. I was absolutely aware of all the positions. My experience told me about what was going on in Kotor Varos, but what I explained to them was that I was not refusing because of my political opinions in order to make them happy. I said, "I am not refusing because of my political opinion, but because I am convinced that I would never return". I knew that if I refuse, I would be killed here in Vrbanja,but it is better that it happens here than in Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you subsequently learn what happened in Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in Kotor Varos part of the population surrendered. Part of the armed population withdrawal towards the mountains, towards the village of Vecici, that was all on Banja Luka TV, and the greatest part of the population was evacuated. For quite a long time they had been under blockade and they had no means to defend themselves,so the majority of the population,all women, children and civilians, men, they were transferred by buses, as I heard on TV, towards Travnik. When that was ended, Kupresanin said on TV on several occasions, "Kotor Varos is now free".

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How were you finally able to leave Vrbanja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I left Vrbanja on 15th January 1993, that is, I tried on several occasions through some people I managed to contact secretly and that live in Vrbanja. I managed to send a message to the International Red Cross and asked to be registered. The message was received and returned, and I was told that they knew I was at Vrbanja but it would be much better if they would not register me. It would be safer for me. I then lost hope of getting out of there but then, as it turned out, some people were trying to get me out of Vrbanja and transfer me to Croatia. I never learned the names of some of those people. I do know some other names. Somewhere towards the beginning of January, in the evening, a young blond woman arrived. She knocked on the door, talked to my sister and she told her she had a piece of paper for me. My sister, when she was sure that there was no danger, called me and on the paper it was said, "Discharge from prison, pursuant to the decision in the official gazette of Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina,from Omarska, discharged, released the following names", and there was a list. There was the No. 8 was the last name, and then by hand there were on the No. 9, 10 and 11 three other names, last one of those names was my name. That woman said that the next morning at 7 o'clock I should go to the company plant which is located in the same house where the International Red Cross is. She said, "Ask for Nine. When that man comes, he will explain to you what you should do next." She told me that in case I did not manage to go to the town, to swallow that piece of paper because the Serb policemen should in no way find out how I got that piece of paper. My sister asked her, "Who are you?" She said, "Well, my sister, I am your sister and his sister; we are all brothers and sisters".

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you require co-operation or assistance from Mr. Kupresanin in order to effect your release?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did he want anything in exchange for his co-operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I did not talk about that with him directly. Mr. Nine, whom I mentioned, talked to him because they knew each other, also the dentist -- I think he might still be in Banja Luka and that is why I will not mention his name, but I think he talked about; if the court wants me, the Tribunal wants me, I can write his name down -- and some other people talked about it. That dentist came and told me that we could obtain such a paper but that in exchange I should write down who I was, how I was, what I did, how I was arrested, how I came to Omarska and how Kupresanin had released me from Omarska, how he brought me to Banja Luka and how I was normally living in Banja Luka and to put in the end that I am grateful to Mr. Kupresanin and thank him for saving my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you provide that letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, I was aware of the risk in case I would not sign that, but I was also aware of the risks of signing the letter. I tried to explain that it would not be good for me to write something like that in case I managed to stay alive and reach Norway -- for some reason, I was constantly saying I would be going to Norway -- in case I arrive there that I would say publicly to the journalist who does what in Banja Luka, that there are people there who save lives and not only those who kill. Two days later, the same gentleman, the dentist, came to me with a text. I did not there sign that text either, but I said if I sign it, in that case Mr. Kupresanin and this dentist could be killed in case somebody finds that in Banja Luka, and that I had a moral obligation to speak the truth and reveal the truth and to say who helped me in what way, and they accepted that explanation and then they abandoned this idea for me to sign the letter. Similar letters were signed, I think, by Mr. Biscevic. I think that he was No. 10 on that list. He was the second one whose name was handwritten on the list and added. It is a young man from Sanski Most. He was brought from Manjaca because he was the son of the dentist's name -- the dentist I mentioned and whose name I did not want to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you finally obtain the necessary document from Mr. Kupresanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The International Red Cross received an oral permission for my evacuation, but the only evacuation arrangement was rejoining of families. That meant that I was a resident of Banja Luka and that part of my family lived in Croatia, so that I could be evacuated to join my family for the family reunion. The problem was that I did not have any kind of documents either with or without photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: May I have this marked for identification as Exhibit 134? (Document handed). (To the witness): Mr. Semenovic, do you recognise this document as the application obtained from Mr. Kupresanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender 134 for admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 134 will be admitted. MR. TIEGER (To the witness): May I ask first that the original be placed on the screen so that the court can take a look at it, and can the translation be placed on? Mr. Semenovic, I noticed that the date listed is 12th January 1992; is that the correct date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the correct date.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Is the year correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Just a second -- no, no, no, the year is not correct. It is 1993, that should be on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: This is the document that Mr. Kupresanin provided for you and that he wanted a letter in exchange for which provided you with an identity paper allowing you to begin the process of leaving Vrbanja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Was it helpful that it identified you as a deputy in the former Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What would the likely effect be if you had found it necessary to show that document at a checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not pass the checkpoint, not even the first one, and there were some 20 checkpoints up to Bosanski Gradica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: During the period of time you were in Vrbanja, what was happening to Muslims in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Refugees were coming to Vrbanja, Muslims from Celinac where the houses had been burned down. Part of the population had been killed, and shortly afterwards arrests started in Bosanska Vrbanja, arrests of Muslims. To start with, it happened in the evening or during the night and later on it started also during the day. At the same time, every time military columns or vehicles would be going through Vrbanja from Celinac towards Banja Luka,there would be quite a lot of shooting and lots of houses were damaged. The grenades were thrown near the mosque and people started getting killed in houses. People lived in fear, completely shut off. They offered the possibility to people to move away, but it was only possible through a private agency by a lady called Perka. She was organising transport from Banja Luka to Serbia or from Banja Luka across Vlasic on the territory under the control of the Bosnian Army, but most of the people did not have the money for it because it cost quite a lot of money.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I do not think we know where Vrbanja is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Semenovic, can you explain where -- I am trying to think, your Honour, which Exhibit might be of -----

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I do not think that will be of assistance. (To the witness): Mr. Semenovic, can you explain where Vrbanja is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is to the east of the Banja Luka. If you look at the centre of the town of Banja Luka and you go towards the east, there is Bosanska Vrbanja. There is just one road and this is the road Banja Luka, Celinac,Kotor Varos,and Bosanska Vrbanja is a suburban part of Banja Luka. It is right at the outskirts near the industrial zone where Incel is. That is where Bosanska Vrbanja starts, along this road I mentioned. The population, the houses, are around the river of Vrbanja that goes into the River Vrbas.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Semenovic, were you finally able to obtain your release from Vrbanja in the Banja Luka region and cross the border on January 15th 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Regardless of the piece of paper I received, I have to say that a different kind of paper it was not possible to obtain. My sister contacted Mr. Granic and the people I mentioned. They said that with this piece of paper I had to go to the Banja Luka SUP, that they should give me a real document. She went there. She asked. She was sent there and there she was told, was she aware who was she asking these documents for and whether this man was still alive. That is what she was asked and that was towards the end of the working day, and just before some kind of a Serb holiday. I decided, regardless of the risk, to start the journey with these documents in the organisation of the International Red Cross, because I expected that the Serb authorities could use me and send me to negotiate with Bosniak Muslims' side, because previously they told me they would take me to Knin, and then that from Knin we should go by the UNPROFOR armed vehicle to the frontline to discuss with the two gentlemen, one of whom was Irfan Ljubijankic, and I knew both of them. I started my journey on 15th January in the morning towards Novska carrying this document, this piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Semenovic. Nothing further, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Cross-examination Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. (To the witness): Mr. Semenovic, you told us this morning that you were entered on that document relating to the Territorial Defence of Trnpolje and that that was your signature. Do you remember seeing the paper this morning? Perhaps we could look at that again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know we can call this up on the computer on A1/7. I was told this yesterday. Perhaps the court official will be able to dial that in?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: This is Defence 6, I believe, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: A1/7. You know more than I do, Mr. Kay. I hope it comes up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a test.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK, we will see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps we can be told which button we press?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, would you help us, please, to get A1/7 on the monitor?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I tried!

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Why do you not just take Defence 6 and we will take a look at the sheet?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let us go back to paper. If the witness can be provided with Defence document 6? (To the witness): Mr. Semenovic, if you could turn to page A1/7 there are numbers and letters in the top right-hand corner. Can you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps a copy of that can be put underneath the light? You told us this morning that you signed this document some four or five days before the conflict at Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, before the first clashes, before the first shots.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. If you would like to look at the other pages relating to the Trnopolje list which start at A1/5, can you see it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And A1/7 where yours is the very last name on the list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You told us this morning that organisation of the Territorial Defence by the local Muslims took some seven days or a week before the first shots were fired at Kozarac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So, before that week are you telling the court that there was no mobilization by the local Territorial Defence unit by the Muslim people at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. May I explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was like this. This is the last stage of the compilation of these lists, and the filing of weaponry. Before that, the TO headquarters had to collect the files from other sources -- well, a decision had to be taken first, a political decision, and then to collect the available files, then compile lists. Then the last step was to go with these lists to the field, door to door, and to offer people to sign it up and to have their weapons put on record if, of course, they wanted to, if there were any to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So shall we look at your answer then in relation to that and see what it means? Are you saying that the lists were compiled some week before the conflict started at Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean these lists?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, but first they were drawn up in the TO headquarters, and then one had to reach every house and show it to people. It was quite an undertaking. I remember that to my house came a young man, Ajdin Zenkic. Usually, those were young people who had nothing better to do and they, therefore, were asked to visit all, to see all the people and show them the lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So you were aware of the organisation that was taking place when this young man knocked on your door; it did not come as a surprise to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew there was the Territorial Defence, and the task of the Territorial Defence is to look after the security and safety of the population. They were instructions issued earlier by the Republican TO headquarters that the Territorial Defence should be mobilized and the population protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Those instructions in relation to the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, when were they issued that they should be mobilized?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the period I am talking about, a month-and-a-half or two months before that. It was possible to do it completely, to round it off, for instance, in Tuzla, in Sarajevo, but in some areas SDS blocked this work, and Prijedor as an example of these areas where the whole process was blocked. Afterwards, it was only possible to organise some parts of the TO in those areas where there still existed or, rather, where the non-Serb population constituted the majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So the instruction for mobilization of the Territorial Defence by the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina was some one-and-a-half to two months before the conflict started at Kozarac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so. I received the information through media, radio Bosnia-Herzegovina and also learned it from people, from government officials, who were involved in this. But at the level of the municipality, before the power was taken over by SDS, it could not be done because SDS blocked it, and we did not want and could not do it in parallel or without SDS. It was simply not possible at the time at the municipal level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The headquarters for the Territorial Defence that we are concerned with here was at Kozarac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The seat, the headquarters of the TO Prijedor, that was the central headquarters for all the neighbourhood,for all the local communes,in the municipality of Prijedor, Prijedor Kozarac, Omarska, Puharska and so on and so forth. So this was the headquarters of the Territorial Defence there because each one of these parts also had its own headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, but your division at Trnopolje, Trnopolje Cesta, the headquarters for that division was in Kozarac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The organisation of the Territorial Defence for these regions around Kozarac came from Kozarac itself, that is where the headquarters was, and that is where the organisation took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, from the TO headquarters. That was the only way possible, permissible by law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, and the Commanding Officer of the headquarters at Kozarac, what was his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You do not know his name? But all those villages around the area of Kozarac that we can see named in the pages of these documents were all organised from Kozarac;is that right? Please look through the pages, if you want, but we can see the villages of Menkovici, if you turn to page 17?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If you turn to page 26 Kozarusa, page 30 Jakupovici, page 36 Dermici, taking a great step through the bundle to 48 Kalata, page 56 Brdjani, again taking a leap through the pages ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Brdjani.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- page 70 Garibi. That is some of the names of these places on these sheets of papers. They were all villages that had as the headquarters Kozarac for the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kozarac Territorial Defence covers the area of Kozarac, several local communes. The headquarters, the central headquarters, is in Kozarac co-ordinating TO units in that area. So, one TO unit is in Trnopolje which again has its smaller units, and the same holds true of other local communes which altogether make Kozarac, that is, the organisation of the Territorial Defence and it was like that for the past 15 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So the document that we are looking at which you have signed at page 7, would that document have been prepared in Kozarac or in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Trnopolje, in Kozarac, we did not have good records. Records were not good anywhere, and this was the first time that the conditions were extraordinary, for the first time since the establishment of the Territorial Defence it was expanded to such an extent, it was the first time. So that there were no lists that could be used ad hoc, but registers, records, were not really good. There were voters lists, there were census records and perhaps some other records. Then these lists, this information, was submitted to the Territorial Defence headquarters in Kozarac. This headquarters, in co-operation with headquarters in Trnopolje,Kamicani and all the other places,then compiled lists of all these people and then it was sent back to the field. As regards the procedure, I really do not know because I am only a member, a rank and file member of the Territorial Defence. In this case, I was not one formally, but now we most of all to do it because this was the only possible response, the only way to try and protect ourselves. Unfortunately, we failed but that was the lawful way through the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So the document we are looking at was typed up at Kozarac, do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I guess so, I guess it was typed in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The information that is on it, which included your name, do you know who in Trnopolje had compiled this list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was done by people in the local commune in the Territorial Defence. I think that Trnopolje had five TO members altogether before the war with five pieces of weaponry. In local communes, that is, neighbourhood communities, there were records. Every village, every hamlet, that is, every part of that community had to be recorded or households had to be recorded. I think that most of these lists were compiled in hand, by hand, because there was no time for anything else. Then it came,I guess, it all was sent to the central headquarters and that they put it in order, they put them in order there and then send it back. I guess that that was the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Before your name was typed on this sheet of paper and before it was presented to you for your signature, had anyone asked you whether you wanted to be a part of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When had you been asked that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All those who carried those lists around were bound, had to ask every person listed whether they were ready and willing to join or not; and some were ill, some simply were unable to. So that everyone who agreed, who gave his free consent, they were signed to the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But my question was when were you asked before this list was typed up whether you wanted to be involved with the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the Prijedor meeting that I already spoke about when ultimatum was given, then a meeting of representatives of all local communes was held, including authorities, local authorities, Reserve police force, police and everybody else. There was only one item on the agenda, what to do. Therefore, the question arose of urgent organisation because there were no plans. Then it was concluded that all able bodied should rally around the Territorial Defence, that records should be made of all the available weapons, that attempts should be made to establish Defence informations of the Territorial Defence which could operate, and an army officer of the former JNA was put in charge of that, including the Territorial Defence, and that was what he tried to do along with people who already were part of the Territorial Defence. After their decision, we knew about that decision, so after that decision it was decided to make records of all this so that he could know how many weapons there were, how much had to be distributed and so on and so forth. I am talking about this. I could see some information -- so I received some information indirectly. Certain things, I had the opportunity to hear, and I was not involved in it personally because I did not belong to the Territorial Defence before that. This was the first time. This was the first time that I accepted to be a member of the Territorial Defence because, from the point of view of formations, I belonged in the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You had had previous army experience in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, like any other soldier who did his military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I expect that other people on the lists that we have before us relating to Trnopolje, some of those had had experience in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All men of age did their military training. It was a legal obligation and could not be evaded. We did not have a professional army in our country. There was, therefore, this compulsory military service. Every man, every boy who came of age before possible further education, that is, before enrolling at university, after turning 18 or 19, every young man went to do his military service. Some did that 30 years ago, some 10 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So the answer was, yes?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think the question was when did Mr. Semenovic decide to become a part of the Territorial Defence, the TO, and it is my understanding, Mr. Semenovic, you decided to become a part of the Territorial Defence after the Prijedor meeting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When was this Prijedor meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some eight days before the war, before the attack of the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Does that help. Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, your Honour, yes. (To the witness): But the organisation that had been taking place in relation to the Territorial Defence for the headquarters in Kozarac, that had been taking place before the Prijedor meeting some eight days before the conflict started; is not that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we knew what the instructions were but we were not able to implement them, objectively speaking, because we did not single out, separate, the Territorial Defence of Kozarac and Prijedor. Before the Serbs took over the power, we had one only Territorial Defence. Our officials were in the Territorial Defence at the municipal level. We did not have two parallel systems. We did not want to have two parallel systems because that would be contravention of the law. So after the military coup, the power was taken over. The municipal Territorial Defence was abolished. All Bosniak Muslims and Croats were evicted from those parts, and parts of it, only segments remained, such as Kozarac Territorial Defence. That is what I am talking about. It was a completely new situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So are you saying then that the research for the names to be involved with the Territorial Defence, the asking of people whether they would be involved, the compilation of all these names in these lists, the indication of what weapons there were, the obtaining of the signatures against most of the names, all took place in the eight days before the conflict? Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The bulk of this work was done some eight days before the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What do you mean the "bulk" of this work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, things that were related to these lists, because it is not a problem. If somebody in Trnopolje was charged with visiting the buildings in Cesta -- we already mentioned it -- that is not a problem. It is about 30 houses on the left and right side of the road. It can be done in two or three hours, and into Kozarac which is four kilometres away. It does not take eight days to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are the names within this list of Trnopolje, Cesta, just Muslim names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are there other ethnic groups? Are there any Serb names within it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are Serb names. There are other ethnic groups on the page that you suggested we look at, that is, A1/7 and 93, Markotic Tone. He is not a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then Sardic under 101, he is not a Muslim either because the Territorial Defence was not, is not a monoethnic formation. Only Serbs left the Territorial Defence in those parts, in those areas, where there was a Muslim majority. I mentioned two or three examples. Under 81, August Majstorovic, 82 Stipe Majstorovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There are the nationalities other than Muslim, are there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. You are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I will put it to you quite simply, Mr. Semenovic, which you can accept or deny, that the organisation of the Territorial Defence with the headquarters at Kozarac had been undertaken considerably before the eight days that you suggest to this court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You may have become involved four or five days before, and your name is the last on the list, is it not, at 106?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this list was all done in one day in the village where I live and where these people listed here, it was done in a matter of a few hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And typed up in few hours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not typed in a few hours, perhaps it took five minutes because they were simply taking the names from the list, but I am saying that it was signed and the signing could take only a few hours, and the compilation of records, the preparation of lists, could also take a few hours. The problem was to find the records, to take down, to take it to Kozarac and take it around and then bring it back to Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And to know who to put on the list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And to know who to put on the list because virtually everyone had signed, had they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of them signed, not all of them but most of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I have a question because I am somewhat confused, Mr. Semenovic. Did the process begin to mobilize the Territorial Defence in Kozarac a month to a month-and-a-half before we see Defence 6 being completed? That is what I understood your testimony to be. I may be confused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will clarify it for you. We mentioned the first day the request, the demands, that the Territorial Defence weapons which were removed and stored in the depot be given back, be returned, to the Territorial Defence staff and to various places in the field, that is, local communes. It took a long time to comply with this request. There was constant communication between the Territorial Defence at the Republican level and the local level and then finally it was done. So some weapons, some pieces of weaponry, a few of them were returned to local communes. This took time. If then this we relate to what we are talking about, then we can say that, yes, it took more than, it took a longer time. But when I said a month-and-a-half before that is related to the Territorial Defence list, but the number, the strength in peace time. At a certain point of time, we faced imminent danger of war and the Territorial Defence can be extended, can be reinforced organisationally. We had a short time at our disposal to strengthen the Territorial Defence and this is this stage and it did not take long. It lasted as long as I told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Which was how long? When was the decision made to strengthen the Territorial Defence in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some seven to 10 days before the war after the Prijedor meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Are there additional questions, Mr. Tieger, in the light of my questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just very quickly, your Honour, and then I will be ready for the recess.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I suppose we can stand in recess for 20 minutes, then perhaps you will have additional questions, perhaps you will have additional questions, Mr. Kay, perhaps Judge Stephen and Judge Vohrah and myself. So we will stand in recess for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Semenovic, if I can follow up on Judge McDonald's questions? After the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina gained international recognition as an independent state, did the presidency, the President of the Republic then order mobilization of the TO forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I am sorry, after the recognition? He prevented mobilization by the army and he ordered the TO mobilization of Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: OK, and is that the order you were referring to earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: After that was there an effort by the SDA in Prijedor to implement that order which was blocked by the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That was prior to the takeover in Prijedor, is that correct, while there was still a lawful legitimate Assembly which was attempting to function under the laws of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: On April 30th then the takeover took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At approximately mid May, you and other SDA leaders had the meeting with Zeljaja during which he threatened to raise Kozarac to the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: After that the Muslims attempted to organise a defensive force by adding to the TO as reflected in the exhibit you were shown?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Semenovic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No further questions, thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: On a quite different subject matter, how was it that non-Serbs were able to disregard mobilization for the conflict in Croatia? I think you said that it was almost exclusively Serbs that answered the mobilization call. Was there not some compulsion involved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. The state leadership of Bosnia-Herzegovina came to the conclusion that the JNA was conducting unlawful movements on operations which have no basis in the law, so that they did unlawful things and that it performed aggression, first, on the Republic of Slovenia and then on the Republic of Croatia. After that decision, after that conclusion, it forbid mobilization into the JNA, that is, they had a political opinion which consisted in saying to people not to go to the army because the JNA was transgressing its authority, and it egressed one of the republics which, according to the constitution, it had to protect. The political opinion of the state leadership was not respected and not realised by the SDS party which had its own political opinion and it called the Serb people to respond positively to mobilization.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, I follow that. Thank you. That explains it. The second question I had was that we have heard very little of the 20 or 30 elected members who represented former communist parties within Prijedor. They, I gather, were strongly against nationalist movements. What did they do when the Serbs took over Prijedor? We know what the SDA did and the SDS. What about those other quite large numbers of members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Politically, it was impossible to do almost anything, and they were treated by the SDS people in the same way as the members of the SDA. They had exactly the same attitude towards them. Wherever they could, that is, in the local commune in Kozarac, those people joined the legitimate legal organs. They were supporting the attitudes of the legal or legal organisation and they were against SDS and against the military coup. Then and after that they were treated equally, and later on after the attack and in the camps most of the political leaders were liquidated during the military operations in the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Generally speaking, what ethnicity were these 20 or 30 former communist members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of them were Bosniak Muslims and a smaller part of them were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. The last question I wanted to ask you was you have spoken of the co-operation between the SDA and the SDS at first partly successful and, ultimately, quite unsuccessful. Did that happen only in Prijedor or was it generally throughout areas within Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Generally within the whole territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Mr. Semenovic, I probably missed this when you started to give your evidence this morning. Do you hold any political office now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What is it, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a member of the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: My second question: Mr. Kay pointed out that your name appeared as the last name in the Territorial Defence list. Is there any significance in that fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there is not. My house is the last in this row of houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any addition questions, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to Mr. Semenovic being permanently excused?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You are permanently excused, Mr. Semenovic. Thank you for coming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Will the Prosecution call their next witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
