utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. The Prosecution will call Mr. Mirsad Mujadzic. MR. MIRSAD MUJADZIC, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Mujadzic, would you please take that oath?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Mujadzic, would you please state your full name for the record?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Mirsad Mujadzic, Mirsad Mujadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born on 7th August 1962.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You were born in Banja Luka in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Where were you raised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was raised from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you attend primary and secondary school in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Where did you go from there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that I studied in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What were your studies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I studied at the Faculty for Medicine and after the Medical School. I did a post graduate course in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What is your current profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Where do you currently work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I work in Sarajevo at the Kosovo Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What is your speciality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a plastic surgeon and I finished my specialisation now in plastic surgery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Where did you begin your medical career?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I started my medical career in Prijedor in 1987, at the Institute for Work Medicine where I worked with a population of workers in nine -- as a general practitioner in the medical offices for Occupational Medicine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In those duties did you travel throughout the opstina to various clinics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The system of work for the Institute of Occupational Medicine was that every two to three months we would go from one surgery to the other. Through my work in occupational medicine, I worked in all nine surgeries for different time lengths in the whole area of the municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Beginning in 1990 did you become involved in politics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Which party did you become affiliated with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I became the member of the party of Democratic Action, the SDA in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What position did you hold in that party in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Prijedor, I was from 17th August 1962 the President of the Municipal Committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In the translation it appears you said 17th August 1962 -- did you mean 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 17th August 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Was that the founding of the SDA in the opstina Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, that was the day of the Founding Assembly of the Municipal Committee in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were you also elected to a position in the Republic Assembly during the general elections in 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was that position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My office was a member of the Council of Citizens in the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you continue both your political duties and your medical practice right up through May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: As a result of your political involvement in the Opstina and the Republic and your position as a medical professional in the opstina Prijedor, did you have the opportunity to meet with many of the Bosnian-Serb political, military and government leaders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did those meetings continue right up through May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Could you tell the court what the ethnic makeup in the opstina Prijedor was prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the war, according to the 1991 census, the ethnic makeup of the Prijedor municipality was the following: 44 per cent Muslim, 42 per cent, 42. 5 per cent Serbs 5- 6 per cent Croats, 5.7 Yugoslavs, and some 2 per cent others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: May I please have this document marked as the next Prosecution Exhibit 135? (Document handed). (To the witness): Dr. Mujadzic, do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What is that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the ethnic representation of various nationalities in the area of the Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And who prepared that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender that document.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 135 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If that could be placed on the screen? (To the witness): Dr. Mujadzic, could you explain the various colours on the map for the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here there are three different colours with which are marked the three nationalities that lived and also their territorial disposition in the municipality of Prijedor; in green there are parts which have been settled by Muslims; in red parts inhabited by Serbs and in blue parts inhabited by Croats. Here we have also got two darker parts in the local commune of Trnopolje. By doing this, I wanted to mark the specificity of this area where very many minorities lived, some 17 different minorities, Ukrainians, Italians, Germans, Russians, Hungarians and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: It appears from the map, as you have created it, that the Serb population had the most territory by settlement, and yet you explained in the ethnic percentage that the Muslims were, in fact, the majority of the population. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is a specificity which is characteristic for the whole Bosnia-Herzegovina in the way people live. Muslims, in general, live in urban parts, in urban areas; whereas Serbs used to live mostly around towns. That means that the areas where Muslims lived are much highly, more densely, populated; whereas the areas where Serbs lived have got less density of population. I also have to mention that this has nothing to do with private ownership, because large areas inhabited by Serbs are very often areas with lots of woods, forests, that belong to the state. So, that there is no correlation between the belonging, the actual property of the area and this colour that I used. This colour means simply where some particular ethnic group lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you. The areas that are denoted by the different colours, were those also recognised as separate traditional areas of settlement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These are only areas where we show how ethnic groups inhabit them, but there are some specificities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you. May I have this document marked next as Prosecution Exhibit 136 and hand it to the witness? (Document handed to the witness).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: As an aside, Mr. Keegan, will the Judges get a copy of the Exhibit 135 colour coded?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I understand they are expensive, but I think it would be helpful. MR. KEEGAN (To the witness): Dr. Mujadzic, do you recognise Prosecution Exhibit 136?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What is that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a representation of the areas traditionally inhabited in Prijedor, because Prijedor is a complex of settlements and here we see several parts from which Prijedor is made of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Could you explain those various areas? I am sorry, excuse me just one moment. Your Honour, I would tender that document.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 136 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you. (To the witness): Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On this document, this central area represents the core of the urban part of Prijedor, and this broken line marks the larger area of the town where some very important infrastructure facilities are located that are necessary for the functioning of the town. Some companies, some factories are there. So we could call this the industrial zone of the town. This zone here is the area of Kozarac. I have to say that Kozarac up until the 60s in this century used to be an independent municipality, and it was a settlement, a town, created much earlier than Prijedor. It dates from the 13th century; whereas Prijedor was founded in the 17th century. So, the population of this area has got very high feeling for identity. The population is mostly Muslim; more than 90 per cent of the population of Kozarac is Muslim. The next area is the area of Omarska. This area is mostly populated by rural population and of Serb areas. It has never been a municipality and there is no urban centre in it. Although in the 80s, between 1980 and 1990, there were some initiatives to found an opstina there. More than 90 per cent of the population is Serb. The next area is the area Ljubija, which before the 60s used to be a municipality. Almost exclusively previously Muslims and Croats used to live there, but after the 2nd World War, a large number of Croats moved to Croatia and because of the iron ore mine in Ljubija some Serbs were settled there. But even today in Ljubija we can determine two subareas, the Donja Ljubija, lower Ljubija, before the Second World War it used to be called Ljubija Islam, but throughout the communist period, this name "Islam" was not used and called Donja Ljubija now, and it is mostly exclusively populated by Muslims, and Gornja Ljubija, upper Ljubija, which today is mostly Croat. The next area is the area of Brda. There is a series of Muslim villages there, except for Rasavci which is populated by Serbs, and there are two other areas with predominant Serb population called Potkozarje and Tomasica. Potkozarje is the part on the edges of the mountain of Kozara. It used to be known as the part with the partisans and resistance. Tomasica is mostly populated by Serbs, there are Serb villages, except for a small part bordering Sanski Most where Croats used to live.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: To aid in the rest of the discussion if I could have this overlay marked as the next Prosecution Exhibit 136A. It is a plastic transparency of 136. If that would be given to the witness and placed on top of 135. Your Honour, I would tender 136A.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The transparency ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection to 136A?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We have not seen it before, but it seems there is no problem. Let me just see what the effect is before we say whether ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you have a copy even of the plastic transparency?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, we have no copy of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: It should be provided. It is a copy of 135. I thought it was given to you. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you have an extra copy, Mr. Keegan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Not of the transparency; just of the paper backing that goes through the copying machine.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Why do you not ask your assistant. Mr. Usher, would you come and get a copy of 136A and you can take a look at that at least, Mr. Wladimiroff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We have no problem here. We accept it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. 136A will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Dr. Mujadzic, these historical areas, of what social significance were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The municipality of Kozarac used to be a municipality before the 60s, but when it became part of the municipality of Prijedor then the whole infrastructure that continued to be built there was transferred to Prijedor, so Kozarac was economically being less advanced. It did not have particular consequences because the municipality was one whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: So, did these merely become points of reference for the people who lived in those areas, in other words, on an area of identification, "I am from Omarska" "I am from Kozarac" regardless of which of the local communes in the area you came from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, normally, as it is the case in many other settlements, one knew that if somebody was from Kozarac he would be normally Muslim, and if somebody came from Omarska he would suppose that the person would be a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did they have any particular relevance to the actual administration of the opstina Prijedor, the government functions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was of no relevance for administrative functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe the history of the relations between the main ethnic groups in the opstina Prijedor prior to 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I should like to mention that during World War II from 1941 to 1942 the municipality of Prijedor made part of the so-called independent state of Croatia NDH, and during that period of time an extremist formation, extremist military formation known as Ustase deported a large part of the Serb population from here, from the territory of the municipality of Prijedor to Jasenovac. The deportation and persecution of the Serb population during World War II was a phenomenon noted throughout the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but in those early days there was a proclamation of Muslim intellectuals in eight towns of Bosnia-Herzegovina to protect the Serb population against persecution. One of the places where the Muslim intellectuals raised their voice to protect the Serb population against persecution was Prijedor. One must say that as of 1942 when Prijedor -- no, when the control of Prijedor was taken over by partisans who at the time were mostly Serbs, at least around Prijedor, in 1942 270 prominent Muslims and Croats were killed in Prijedor and likewise in the municipality of Kozarac. In 1945 when a partisan unit from Montenegro was passing through Kozarac about 300 people were killed. The area of Brdo and Ljubija were mostly left aside, that is neither Ustase nor partisans did much harm there. So this is the area which is historically called Potkozarje, it is a traditional partisan territory, and during World War II there were no Chetniks there. This is the famous insurgent Potkozarje. Some Chetniks or some Chetnik villages could be found in the historical part of Prijedor called Omarska. I am sorry, could you please rectify the map? Will you please adjust the map?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: For the benefit of the interpreters could you please slow down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So this is the lower, this is the area of Donja and Gornja Marica, Gradina, Jelicka, Mijevici. However, generally speaking one can say that in Prijedor there were no major ethnic, local ethnic conflicts amongst Serbs, Croats and Muslims, and that Prijedor is understood to be a partisan town and in Potkozarje a famous partisan reel originated. It is a dance when people hold each other by hand and it epitomized brotherhood and unity which was the basis, the A-B-C of ideology in Tito's Yugoslavia. In this manner Prijedor came to symbolize the brotherhood unity of the former Yugoslavia at large, because when compared with other towns in Bosnia-Herzegovina there were no major inter-ethnic conflicts. So that in Tito's time, that is since the 50s until the late 80s or the turn of the decade, the inter-ethnic relationships in Prijedor were very good indeed. There were many mixed marriages. It was a normal phenomenon, a common thing, that good friendships existed, were struck between Muslims, Croats Serbs. It hardly ever occurred to people to think what ethnic group who belonged to. We lived in a normal idyllic tranquillity. Excellent inter-ethnic and religious tolerance reigned. Not without reason Ante Markovic, and he was the Prime Minister in the former Yugoslavia in the early 90s and he was the driving force behind very many reformist tendencies and undertakings in the former Yugoslavia and was also a man who tried to preserve the unity of Yugoslavia, began his electoral campaign as the leader of reformist forces aspiring to preserve the unity of Yugoslavia. He began this campaign in Prijedor in Mrakovica as symbol of brotherhood and unity in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Against this background of a non-divided lifestyle in Prijedor, did you begin to see the rise of Serb nationalism in the late 1980s?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first initial changes which struck the eye, which were visible in the daily life, they began to emerge in 1986 to 1987. In 1987 an event marked those changes and that was Agrokomerc scandal when the Vice President of the former Yugoslavia, Hamdija Pozderac was ousted from office, at the time he was also the Chairman of the Constitution Commission for the change for amendments to the constitution, and a number of other events followed suit which, in political terms, clearly indicated the evolution of Serb nationalism. Among the ordinary folk one could see it, one could guess it by hearing the singing of Serb nationalistic songs from time to time, and some changes in the marking of individual historical events, attacks on the principles underlying Yugoslavia, and this gradually began to make its way into media propaganda which was clearly directed from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What were some of the ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So that people began to discuss these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What were some of the significant political events which indicated the rise of Serb nationalism? You indicated the ousting of the Vice President of Yugoslavia at the beginning of 1987. What happened at the 8th Central Committee meeting in 1988?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the 8th session of the Central Committee of the League of Communists of Serbia Dragisa Pavlovic and Ivan Stambolic were removed from office. They represented the moderate political and the moderate political stream in Serbia, and they accepted the fundamentals of the constitutional principle of 1974 which spelt out the equality of the peoples in Yugoslavia. This was the basis, these were the foundations of Tito's Yugoslavia throughout his rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Who was the ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This change was executed by Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Why did Milosevic want to oust the existing government in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because they accepted the constitutional principles of 1974 as regards their way of principles and changes that he wanted to bring about, and that was the constitution of Yugoslavia on principles that would be significantly different, that is the principle of one citizen one vote. In this manner Serbia would gain absolute predominance in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: So, Slobodan Milosevic wanted to establish a constitutional amendment which would give the right of one vote one person for the changes to the constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The former Yugoslavia was made of six republics and two provinces, and irrespectively of the size every republic had an equitable number of seats in the Federal Parliament. So that, for instance, a small Montenegro with a population of only about 600,000 had the same number of seats in the Federal Parliament as Serbia with a population of over 8 million. But this was a way to preserve mutual equality of the peoples of ethnic groups in the former Yugoslavia, and it was this that Milosevic wanted to remove.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: After the ousting of the moderate government in Serbia and the rise of Milosevic, you indicated there was then propaganda which began to come out of Serbia. What was the nature of that propaganda?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The propaganda came from all media, as is usual, television to begin with, Television Belgrade in this particular case, written press, papers, Politika Ekspres and Politika, they were regime papers, exclusively Radio Belgrade and in yet another way which became a new form, a new manifestation of political propaganda in these newly emerging situations, and there were the so-called rallies, mass rallies, popular rallies where speeches, addresses were delivered with nationalist chauvinistic content.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was one such speech at Gazimestan in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, after the 8th session from which Milosevic came out as an absolute victor and when he thus removed this complete moderate stream in Serbia, as symbolized by Stambolic and Pavlovic, a mass rally was held at Gazimestan, this is Kosovo, at a place where in 1389 the battle took place between the Turkish army and the Serb army; in other words, the occasion was the 600th anniversary of the battle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was the most well-known part of Milosevic's speech?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During that big rally there were about 2 million Serbs from all over Yugoslavia, and the driving power or rather the message of the rally was: "I shall not allow anyone to beat the Serb people." Milosevic thus wanted to appear as the protector, the patron of all Serbs, regardless of the republic that those Serbs lived in in the former Yugoslavia. The message of that whole rally and the reason why this was done on Kosovo and on the 600th anniversary is twofold. Milosevic wanted to point out, and the Serbia propaganda then commented on it like this, that 600 years ago, as they said, the valiant Serbian army stopped at that very place, the breakthrough of Islam. That was the second very important message which Milosevic wanted to send from that rally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What effect did this rally have on the image and popularity of Milosevic amongst the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A long time before that meeting the territory of the former Yugoslavia of the republics inhabited by Serbs were flooded by Milosevic's photographs, badges, slogans, flags, stickers, and the rally was attended by Serbs from Bosnia and Croatia with buses with his posters plastered all over, that is recognisable iconography, recognisable imagery, and indicating the evolution of the personality cult, that is promotion of Milosevic into the absolute leader of the Serb people wherever they might be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: At the 14th Communist Congress in 1989 what was the major debate over?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For that Congress Milosevic used those mass rallies to remove from office the leadership in Vojvodina in Kosovo, in Montenegro. He brought in his men. So that the 14th Congress of the League of Communists of the former Yugoslavia he came to this Congress already holding tremendous political power. The gist of the happenings at the 14th Congress of the League of Communists was the discussion about the fundamentals of the constitution of 1974, that is the one person one vote principle, and if that principle were adopted it would have signified the end of equality of the nations in the former Yugoslavia, thus abolishing the fundamental principle which governed the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What were the reactions of some of the republic candidates at this Congress to the positions put forth by Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the close of the 14th Congress the Slovenian leadership left the League of Communists of Yugoslavia. One still remembers the face incontinence of Sonja Lokar, a member of the process of League of Communists of Slovenia who left the hall, the Congress crying in tears, indicating that they were leaving the Congress because they had been compelled because the principle of the equality of the peoples was no longer accepted because Milosevic wanted to abolish it. Croatia too left the 14th Congress, the Croatian delegation left the 14th Congress but did not leave the League of Communists of Yugoslavia. The delegation of Bosnia-Herzegovina did the same, whereas other delegations from other republics and provinces attended the Congress to the end, even though it adopted no final conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: As we move into 1990 then, what was the effect of all of this propaganda and these political debates on everyday life in the opstina Prijedor and elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before that, before 1990, that is ever since 1987, since the Agrokomerc scandal to so-called popular happenings, that is street rallies, massive street rallies, the purpose of which was in Vojvodina, Kosovo and Montenegro to remove from office the lawful leaderships which was Milosevic's typical proscription for the change of authorities, and Milosevic attempted a similar, tried a similar recipe in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in Slovenia. However, the Slovenian leadership said they would not allow similar rallies and Bosnia-Herzegovina sent a similar answer. In Prijedor itself where the ethnic composition already said 44 per cent Muslim, 42.5 per cent Serbs and 5.6 Croats, there was polarization which took place but it did not quite follow the ethnic principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What principle did it follow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a matter of fact there were two blocks which were formed, two blocks emerged. One was made of Serbs lending full support to Milosevic's policy and embracing him, accepting him already as their political leader, and the second block was made of non-Serbs, that is all the others who did not espouse Milosevic's policy and could not reconcile themselves and could not come to terms with the principles underlying that policy. In everyday life people were already obsessed with stories about pro and against, for and against Milosevic. In factories, in pubs, in restaurants, in everyday life, in every walk of everyday life one could feel this polarization.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Within this atmosphere what were the driving principles in the founding of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Evidently this policy as pursued by Milosevic threatened, endangered the basic principles of democracy and in 1990 in the former Yugoslavia as a result of processes which were taking place throughout the former East European camp bloc, people began to be democratically aware and they began to be aware that democratization, that democratic changes were needed. The party of the Democratic Action, as it is name says, is a political organisation which emerged in order to fight for democracy, like a series of other parties, and among other things as one of the fronts which had to resist the growing threat to democracy coming from the east from Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was the basic platform of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a nutshell, one could say democracy, that is SDA advocated and continues to advocate democracy, a free market, and respect all human rights, including ethnic rights, religious rights, cultural rights and all other human rights based and understanding Europe and the whole democratic world.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we move into a new area this might be a convenient place to stop.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will adjourn until Wednesday, May 29th at 2.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: (The court adjourned until Wednesday, 29th May 1996).

procedural_notes.text: (The court adjourned for a short time)
